This paper presents a novel, streamlined proof of the well-established result regarding the reduced cohomology of the Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum $K(\mathbb{F}_2, n)$. Specifically, it demonstrates that the Steenrod square operations $\{Sq^I\}$ residing in degrees $2^{n} \leq |Sq^I| < 3 \cdot 2^{n} - 2^{n+1}$ constitute a basis for the reduced mod-2 cohomology ring of the spectrum $K(\mathbb{F}_2, n)$.

The primary goal of the proposed project is to develop a specialized filter for the Lyman-alpha spectral line, enabling the detection of high-redshift galaxies and the early universe. This initiative involves designing and fabricating a filter that offers high transmission in the Lyman-alpha band while effectively suppressing background noise from the Sun and Earth. To achieve this, the team will design and create a high-performance optical filter using advanced thin-film coating technologies. This work will include designing the filter, simulating its spectral properties, and conducting laboratory testing to verify its performance. Ultimately, the resulting device is expected to serve as a prototype for future space-based observatories, such as the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, which will utilize similar technology to study the early cosmos.

This paper addresses the optimal management of graph symmetric systems, a framework that extends the well-established theory of Markovian lumpability to the broader realm of ergodic systems. We demonstrate that for these graph symmetric systems, the optimal management task can be executed using a distributed approach via graph filters. To achieve this, we introduce a graph filter framework capable of generating the requisite statistics for optimal management. We prove that this framework can be deployed through a distributed algorithm utilizing only local information exchange. Furthermore, we show that the graph filter is able to compute the sufficient statistics necessary for both graph symmetric system management and for assessing the degree of graph symmetry. We also establish that the graph filter can determine the optimal solution for graph filtering itself. Finally, we validate the graph filter framework's efficacy in executing graph symmetric system management and in detecting graph symmetric structures.

Image indexing involves the automatic categorization of images into groups based on their visual resemblance. While traditional methods typically rely on a static set of tags, this approach fails to capture the inherent relational context among images within a collection. We introduce a novel methodology for dynamic image indexing that leverages a graph structure to explicitly model these inter-image relationships. In this framework, nodes represent individual images, while edges signify the degree of visual similarity between them. We propose a learning algorithm capable of automatically determining edge weights by analyzing pairs of images. This dynamic indexing system is designed to be continuously updated as new images are introduced, with the specific objective of enhancing the precision of a pre-existing index. We evaluate this system against a baseline static method using both a large-scale dataset of 1.5 million images and a smaller, curated set of 1,000 images. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly surpasses the static approach in performance.

This paper introduces keyless verification for the wiretap and additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel models. In keyless verification, the receiver determines the authenticity of a sender without prior shared secrets, relying solely on the channel characteristics. We present keyless verification schemes for both the wiretap and AWGN channel models. In the wiretap scenario, the receiver verifies a message by generating a codeword from a specific codebook; the receiver accepts the message if the codeword is received with high probability, but rejects it if the message is received with low probability. We examine the dispersion-free transport of charged particles within periodic potentials, specifically focusing on the influence of varying charge magnitudes and potential depths. Our findings indicate that, for a fixed potential depth, increasing the charge magnitude expands the stable regions associated with dispersionless motion. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the existence of such stable regions is contingent upon the ratio of potential depth to charge magnitude exceeding a specific critical threshold.

This study introduces a novel method for evaluating impulse responses, utilizing local projections to capture the nonlinear relationship between response variables and time since a shock. By employing a flexible functional form, the approach accommodates complex response patterns, including non-monotonicity, varying degrees of persistence, and asymmetrical reactions to positive versus negative shocks. Simulations confirm that the estimator performs robustly across diverse scenarios. Additionally, an application to US macroeconomic data demonstrates the method's effectiveness in estimating post-2008 financial crisis responses, revealing significant non-monetary effects that persist for multiple years and exhibit distinct asymmetry.

We investigate the angular Casimir torque exerted on a test charge $q$ situated within a dielectric cylinder of radius $R$ and relative permittivity $\epsilon_r$, which is coaxially enclosed by an outer dielectric cylinder of relative permittivity $\epsilon'_r$. The analysis demonstrates that this quantum vacuum fluctuation-induced torque scales linearly with the test charge, allowing it to be modeled as an effective angular dipole moment. Furthermore, the derived torque expression incorporates the quantum electrodynamic (QED) correction to the classical Coulomb interaction.

Fine-grained named entity recognition (NEC) entails identifying predefined subtypes for specific entity classes, such as distinguishing between "cities" and "countries" under the broader category of "locations." While prior research has primarily focused on enhancing recognition rates, it has largely overlooked the quality of subtype discrimination. To address this gap, we introduce FGNET-RH, a novel framework designed to improve NEC accuracy through subtype discrimination within a hyperbolic space. This approach leverages the intrinsic properties of hyperbolic geometry to efficiently model hierarchical relationships among fine-grained entities. The framework comprises two key modules: (1) a hyperbolic embedding module that utilizes Poincaré representations to capture subtype relationships, and (2) a refinement module that utilizes both Euclidean and hyperbolic spaces to boost overall accuracy. Experimental results on the FB15 dataset demonstrate that FGNET-RH achieves an F1-score of 84.15%, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art by 1.15%. Furthermore, the model exhibits superior performance in discriminating fine-grained subclasses compared to existing methods.

This paper focuses on the general class $\mathcal{S}$, defined by the conditions $f(0)=0$, $f'(0)=1$, and the existence of analytic functions $u$ and $v$ within the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$ such that $f$ takes the specified integral form. We establish upper bounds for the second Hankel determinant associated with the analytic function $f$ within this class. Additionally, we derive sharp upper bounds specifically for the subclass $\mathcal{U}$, which consists of functions $f$ in $\mathcal{S}$ satisfying $|w(z)-1|<1$ for all $z$ in $\mathbb{D}$.

Cloud data centers face significant challenges in meeting the growing demand for cloud services, particularly regarding the efficient allocation of resources. To address this, we introduce "Prepartition," a novel resource allocation strategy that optimizes the fulfillment of virtual machine (VM) requests while accounting for user preferences for specific hardware types and the timing of requests. By enabling users to reserve and pre-assign resources, the system reduces the overhead associated with dynamic scheduling. Our approach distributes these VMs across racks to minimize the total number of active racks, thereby lowering energy consumption. Additionally, we have developed a heuristic algorithm capable of efficiently handling large volumes of VM requests. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques in both energy efficiency and the rate of successfully fulfilled VM requests.

Forecasting the future equilibrium of dynamic systems is essential across numerous disciplines, including economics, social sciences, and machine learning. However, this task is difficult because equilibrium states are often implicit, defined only by fixed-point conditions rather than explicit formulas. This study introduces a novel fixed-point network designed to forecast these equilibria in time-varying environments. The model comprises two primary components: a recurrent network that captures temporal patterns to generate a prediction function, and an auxiliary network tasked with estimating the system's Jacobian at the anticipated equilibrium. The architecture is trained using an auxiliary loss function that enforces the system's fixed-point constraints. Empirical evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method effectively learns to forecast complex equilibrium behaviors.

This paper investigates the bounds on causal influences within a fixed causal structure. We present a straightforward algorithm that generates a bound on the influence of any specific cause given a set of observed variables in a causal graph. Our approach is rooted in the factorization of the joint distribution over causes and effects, utilizing the bounds of observed conditional distributions to constrain influence values. We demonstrate that this methodology is highly effective for high-dimensional settings, such as images, by applying it to a convolutional neural causal model. In these experiments, the algorithm successfully narrows the range of influences in a manner that is consistent with human intuition.

This paper introduces a novel framework for monitoring linear time-invariant systems subjected to state attacks. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on bounding the distance between the true and estimated states, our method utilizes prediction error to track system behavior. We first derive an upper bound on the worst-case prediction error caused by bounded attacks and then transform this error into the original state space using a change of coordinates. This coordinate transformation yields a new, potentially unstable monitoring system where the state represents the prediction error. To ensure robustness, we design a dynamic gain for this monitoring system that remains invariant to specific attack-induced perturbations. This approach guarantees that the gain is attack effective within a defined region, ensuring the system's stability even when stealthy attacks are present.

Natural language summarization is a critical task in information retrieval, yet a lack of resources for Indian languages hinders its application in those tongues. This study introduces GAE-ISumm, an unsupervised summarization system designed for these languages. The approach employs a graph-based algorithm to generate concise summaries from input text. Evaluations on the newly created GENE-ISumm dataset demonstrate that the model achieves a ROUGE-1 score of 0.40, a ROUGE-2 score of 0.23, and a ROUGE-L score of 0.28.

This paper examines s-rings of degree 4 that are isomorphic to the polynomial ring in one variable over an s-ring of degree 2. We establish that such structures necessarily possess an infinite center and provide examples of infinite s-rads of infinite cardinality.

This study investigates the possibility of massive, unseen companions orbiting five nearby stars (Procyon, Sirius, Alpha Centauri A, Beta Centauri, and Alpha Draconis) that could account for the observed acceleration in their motions. By analyzing the astrometric data from Gaia DR2, we determine the masses and distances of these potential hidden objects. Our findings reveal that the unseen companions to Procyon, Sirius, and Alpha Centauri A are significantly more massive than the primary stars, with estimated masses of 1.04 ± 0.05, 1.03 ± 0.05, and 1.03 ± 0.05 solar masses respectively, and distances of 8.6 ± 0.1, 2.6 ± 0.1, and 11.0 ± 0.1 parsecs respectively. In contrast, the unseen companions to Alpha Centauri B and Beta Centauri are less massive than their primaries, with estimated masses of 0.96 ± 0.04 and 0.96 ± 0.04 solar masses respectively, and distances of 11.0 ± 0.1 and 390 ± 10 parsecs respectively. These results suggest that the observed acceleration is likely caused by the gravitational influence of these unseen companions.

Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) have become a standard tool for unsupervised learning of latent representations. While regularization techniques like dropout are commonly used to enhance their generalization, this study introduces a VAE variant incorporating L1 and L2 norms as explicit regularizers. We further analyze these new models using the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm, demonstrating that the Bayes Information Criterion (BIC) can effectively identify the optimal number of latent dimensions. Experimental results on the MNIST dataset confirm that the proposed regularized VAEs achieve superior performance compared to both standard VAEs and Variational Autoencoders equipped with dropout.

The proliferation of IoT devices has introduced significant security risks, particularly for critical infrastructure like smart homes. This paper introduces a private blockchain-based monitor designed to enhance the security of IoT gadgets within residential environments. The proposed system leverages a centralized monitor equipped with a localization module to track device positions and ensure they remain within designated safe zones. By utilizing a private blockchain, the system maintains a secure, immutable ledger of device activities, thereby preventing unauthorized access and tampering. The solution is implemented using Hyperledger Fabric, a private blockchain framework, and has been validated through a simulation involving 100 devices. The results demonstrate that the proposed architecture effectively enhances the security of IoT devices in smart home applications.

This paper introduces a deep learning-based approach to quantizing the log-likelihood (L) variables in soft-decoding algorithms for optical communication systems. The proposed method employs a neural network to determine optimal quantization bit depths for L-flip pairs, aiming to minimize the Bit Error Rate (BER) under a fixed bit budget. The study evaluates this method using a 16-QAM system with 100 Gbit/s transmission over a standard single-mode fiber (SSMF) channel. The results demonstrate that the proposed deep learning-based bit allocation achieves BER performance nearly identical to that of full soft-decoding, while reducing the decoding complexity by a factor of 100.

This study investigates parameterized approaches to the challenge of determining whether a directed acyclic graph (DAG) admits an upward planar embedding. An upward planar drawing is defined as one where edges follow an upward trajectory and no edges intersect, save at their common start or end points. Our findings include an algorithm capable of resolving this problem within $O^*(2^k)$ time, where $k$ signifies the count of the graph's bridges. Additionally, we demonstrate that the task remains W[1]-hard when parameterized specifically by treewidth.

Crowdsourcing has emerged as a cost-effective method for gathering large volumes of data, yet it introduces significant challenges due to the inherent variability in annotator expertise and motivations. This study investigates these issues by analyzing a real-world dataset for image classification, where human annotation patterns are represented through a "human softmax" distribution. We evaluate an ensemble model designed to estimate the probability of uncertain labels, aiming to filter out noisy data before it hinders machine learning performance. Our findings indicate that the proposed ensemble effectively predicts uncertain annotations, thereby reducing the impact of data errors on model training.

We demonstrate that the norm of the transfer operator for a hyperbolic flow decreases exponentially, provided the operator is defined on spaces of anisotropic distributions. This outcome extends prior findings by Baladi and by Nowicki and Riveralet, which addressed the discrete-time case. As a direct application, we derive the existence of a discrete spectrum for the $L^2$-density of the semiflow's invariant measure.

A $\lambda$-covering array of strength $t$ and index $N$ is an $n \times N$ array where every $\lambda \times t$ sub-table appears at least once. This paper addresses the problem of determining the minimum index $N$ for given values of $n$ and $t$, specifically focusing on strength-$2$ arrays. We introduce a new upper bound on this minimum index and evaluate it against current records for specific parameter sets. Additionally, we present a general algorithm for constructing covering arrays that is simple to implement and often yields structures with an optimal or near-optimal index.

Nonlocal games involving maximally correlated states are a specific subset of the broader category of correlation games. In this study, we demonstrate that for the sub-class of games defined by the noisy box scenario—where the shared resource is a noisy version of the maximally correlated state—there exists an algorithm capable of determining the optimal winning probability. This result is achieved by reducing the problem to the computation of the optimal value within a particular convex optimization framework.

This paper partially replicates the work of Li et al. (2019), who developed a genetic algorithm for automatically reproducing software crashes. The original study evaluated the tool on 100 crash bugs from the Firefox suite and reported a success rate of 60%. Our results indicate that the tool successfully resolved 50 of the 100 test cases, matching their reported figure exactly. However, we identified a significant discrepancy in their reporting for cases 11 and 12; they claimed success where our analysis confirms failure. Furthermore, we discovered that the tool's output incorrectly labeled cases 11 and 12 as successful despite failing to resolve the crashes.

The nature of the superconducting state in cuprates remains a subject of debate, with recent theories proposing a complex mixture of $d$-wave and $s$-wave pairing. To investigate this, we performed a scanning tunneling microscope study on optimally doped Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_{8+\delta}$ (Bi-2212) in the superconducting regime. Our results reveal that the vortex core structure is dominated by an emerging $s$-wave component, which significantly influences the density of states at the vortex center. Furthermore, we identified a novel phase transition between two distinct vortex grid configurations: one characterized by alternating square and square grids, and the other by alternating square and rectangular grids.

This study investigates thermal photon anisotropic flow within the framework of relativistic hydrodynamics, utilizing a shear-to-shear ratio of $\eta/s = 0.09$ and a bulk-to-shear ratio of $\zeta/s = 0.1$. The analysis reveals that thermal photon $v_2$ and $v_3$ flow coefficients are highly sensitive to the anisotropic expansion of the quark-gluon plasma. By examining the transverse momentum dependence of these coefficients, the QGP's viscous characteristics can be extracted, offering a complementary perspective to existing studies on thermal photon flow.

We investigate the magnetic ordering of the Kagome and triangular lattices within the framework of the Heisenberg model, utilizing a variational approach to construct ordered states and calculate their energies. Our analysis reveals that the ground state is governed by the ratio of nearest-neighbor ($J_1$) to next-nearest-neighbor ($J_2$) exchange couplings. Specifically, when $J_1/J_2$ is small, the system favors a 120-degree ordered state; conversely, large ratios lead to ferromagnetic ordering. In the intermediate regime, we identify two distinct phases: a non-collinear state featuring magnetic unit cells twice as large as the lattice, and a collinear state with a unit cell matching the lattice size. Our results indicate that the stability of the collinear phase is highly sensitive to the model's anisotropy.

This paper addresses the challenge of estimating average treatment effects in large-scale experiments where treatment assignments are controlled, yet outcomes remain subject to random variation. We introduce a new class of post-selection estimators that maintain false discovery rate (FDR) control under arbitrary dependence among outcomes, even when applied to the entire population of treated units. These estimators are constructed by selecting from among various candidate estimators, each corresponding to a specific subset of units. We establish that our method achieves consistent average treatment effect estimation under mild conditions, provided the proportion of selected units does not vanish. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our estimator admits valid representation as a convex combination of estimators derived from all possible treated-unit subsets, a property that facilitates the development of efficient computational algorithms. Finally, we show that our estimator can achieve optimal minimax rates of convergence in specific scenarios.

This paper examines the foundational principles of cosmic expansion, including the Friedmann equations, the cosmological constant, and the evolution of the universe. It explores the dynamics of the cosmos across different epochs, analyzing the roles of matter, radiation, and dark energy. Furthermore, it addresses current observational evidence for dark energy, discusses potential theoretical models, and evaluates their implications for the ultimate fate of the universe.

We investigate the potential compatibility of type-X two-Higgs-doublet models (2HDM) with experimental anomalies in the $W$ boson mass and the muon's anomalous magnetic moment. Our analysis indicates that a light pseudoscalar, with a mass below 100 GeV, can simultaneously address the muon $(g-2)$ anomaly and the $W$ boson mass discrepancy. This scenario is particularly favored by the CMS measurement of the diphoton signal at 750 GeV, which aligns with the pseudoscalar's mass. We further examine the model's viability against existing experimental constraints and determine that the best-fitting parameter space remains largely unexplored by the LHC Run 2 data.

Software maintenance and development are heavily dependent on code search, where developers locate relevant sections by querying identifiers. However, the absence of adequate information in existing repositories often leads to incomplete search results. To address this, we introduce QUICKAR, a novel approach that automatically rewrites code searches by drawing upon crowd-sourced data to enhance the retrieval of relevant code. By integrating information from commit messages, file histories, and pull requests, QUICKAR identifies missing identifiers in a query and generates expanded inquiries. Our evaluation across three open-source projects demonstrates that QUICKAR successfully augments queries with an average of 2.6 additional identifiers, thereby increasing the number of relevant matches found.

Entrainment refers to the phenomenon where interlocutors subconsciously mirror each other's speech patterns, including prosody, word choice, and speaking rate. This study introduces an unsupervised metric for quantifying entrainment in spontaneous dialogue, grounded in a deep neural network (DNN) trained to classify utterances as belonging to the same speaker. We evaluate this metric across three datasets: two featuring continuous speech from the Spontaneous Conversational Speech Database and one featuring turn-by-turn data from the Spontaneous Conversational Speech Database. Results indicate a strong positive correlation between the unsupervised metric and a traditional rate-based measure of entrainment. Additionally, we demonstrate that unsupervisedly computing entrainment across varying temporal windows yields results consistent with established hypotheses regarding the persistence of entrained effects.

We introduce an updated version of the RCESeDv2 framework, designed to handle both spectral and imaging data. This version features two primary web-based tools: a data visualization tool and a data exploration tool. The visualization tool allows users to view spectral and imaging data, generate data representations, and export them. The exploration tool enables filtering, searching, and downloading of data from the Spectral Image Data Collections (SIDC). The exploration tool is currently integrated into the Spectral Image Data Collections (SIDC) and is accessible at https://sidc.astro.ucla.edu/.

Temporal action segmentation involves partitioning an entire video into distinct segments, each corresponding to a specific action. While prior research has largely concentrated on supervised methods, unsupervised approaches remain a significant challenge. This study introduces SSCAT, an unsupervised framework designed to automatically segment actions within unlabeled data. The method leverages self-supervised learning to generate action representations by modeling the co-occurrence patterns of visual features extracted from the video. Additionally, a novel regularization technique is employed to enhance the quality of a binary mask, which delineates the action regions. The approach demonstrates superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods on the Charades-Extracted benchmark, achieving an Action Mean Average Precision (mAP) of 27.6% and an Action Mean Accuracy (mAcc) of 27.6%.

The recent discovery of the $P_c(4450)$ pentaquark by the LHCb collaboration has reignited interest in exotic hadronic matter. This work investigates the production of hidden-charm di-hadrons and pentaquarks within $B$-meson decays, employing a framework of quark-level current algebra. The study demonstrates that the $B$ decays into the $J/\psi$ and a $\Sigma$ baryon, alongside the $B$ decays into the $D$ and a $\Lambda$ baryon, exhibit a significant enhancement in amplitude due to the presence of intermediate, off-shell, concealed-charm pentaquark states. Theoretical predictions for the branching ratios of these decay channels are provided. Furthermore, the study analyzes the subsequent decays of the $J/\psi\Sigma$ and $D\Lambda$ systems into their respective final states, offering a detailed examination of the underlying mechanisms. The results indicate that the $B$ decays into the $J/\psi\Sigma$ and $D\Lambda$ final states are suppressed by approximately two orders of magnitude relative to the corresponding two-body production processes.

This paper introduces a new instructional feedback mechanism for software testing education, designed to help students grasp core concepts through targeted questioning. By prompting learners to engage in conceptually focused inquiries, this approach aims to deepen their understanding of testing principles. The study validates the effectiveness of this method through an empirical evaluation involving 100 undergraduate participants, who were randomly assigned to one of three groups: Inquiry-Based Conceptual Feedback (IBCF), Traditional Thorough Feedback (TTF), or a Control group receiving no feedback. The findings indicate that both IBCF and TTF groups demonstrated superior performance compared to the control group. Furthermore, the TTF group achieved significantly higher results than the IBCF group. These outcomes suggest that while IBCF is beneficial, TTF remains more effective in enhancing students' grasp of testing fundamentals.

Source-free domain adaptation (SDA) has emerged as a critical challenge in deep learning, particularly when the source domain's data is inaccessible due to privacy restrictions. While recent methods have largely focused on semi-supervised SDA by generating pseudo-labels to address source-domain unlabeled inputs, this approach is often impractical in real-world scenarios where such data cannot be stored. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel framework termed Hypothesis Shift (HS). Instead of relying on source-domain pseudo-labels, HS leverages unlabeled data from the target domain to construct a "Hypothesis Shift" (HS) model. This model is designed to minimize the discrepancy between the source and target domains by aligning their respective hypothesis distributions. Furthermore, we incorporate a semi-supervised learning component to refine the alignment of these distributions. Comprehensive experiments across various domain adaptation benchmarks demonstrate that HS consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

Gas-core nuclear thermal rocket engines are being investigated as a means to reduce travel time for deep space missions. This paper examines the current state of the art, outlining the fundamental design principles, the primary physical mechanisms at work, and the critical unresolved issues. Furthermore, the discussion covers the leading proposed configurations, the essential components of a functional system, and the anticipated performance metrics.

Atmospheres of exoplanets and brown dwarfs are composed of numerous molecular species, each featuring a vast array of spectral lines. To facilitate the analysis of spectra from these objects, we have created EXOPLINES, a comprehensive archive of molecular line lists and cross-sections tailored for spectral modeling. This database supports simulations across a wide range of temperatures (500–3,000 K) and pressures (10⁻⁶–10⁴ bar). We have compiled data for 12 species—including H₂O, CH₄, NH₃, HCN, CO, CO₂, H₂, HD, H₂S, CS, CS₂, and NaH—utilizing the HITRAN and ExoMol databases. For each species, we provide line lists, temperature-dependent absorption cross-sections, and precomputed k-rings at various pressure levels. The EXOPLINES archive is accessible via http://exo.lines-exo.org.

We introduce a novel groundness predicate for Answer Set Programing (ASP) that is defined inductively, adhering to the standard inductive definitions of atoms and ground terms while respecting the syntactic separation between object and meta-variables. We demonstrate that this predicate aligns with the conventional notion of groundness found in logic programming literature, which operates under the assumption that object and meta-variables are disjoint. Furthermore, we show that this groundness predicate can be effectively integrated into the stable model semantics by modifying the reduct operation. This integration yields a unified semantic framework applicable to both first-order and propositional ASP, thereby generalizing existing results that were previously limited to the propositional case.

We introduce the initial law governing quantum resource theories, which extends the well-established framework for quantum operations and states. This law provides a systematic method for defining and establishing operational measures of resources. Specifically, it establishes measurement procedures that bound the cost of generating a specific resource and the benefit derived from utilizing it. We demonstrate the approach by deriving existing results for entanglement, thermodynamic resources, and asymmetry, while also applying it to establish novel bounds for coherence.

We introduce a method for estimating unknown data distributions using only moment information. This approach is applicable to various data types, including real numbers, vectors, and matrices, and is utilized to address several statistical learning challenges. Specifically, we develop a technique for estimating the covariance matrix of a real-valued matrix that is more precise than previous methods. Additionally, we present an algorithm for estimating the top-$k$ singular vectors of a large matrix derived from a known moment, which offers superior accuracy compared to existing solutions. Finally, we describe a procedure for estimating the top-$k$ eigenvectors of a Hermitian matrix based on moment data, achieving better performance than prior approaches.

This study addresses Bayesian inference challenges within heavy-tailed multivariate time series, focusing on scenarios where the series dimensions are high, the series length is moderate, and the series length is low. We introduce a multivariate extension of the Gamma autoregressive model, which allows for flexible, data-driven estimation of the degrees of freedom characterizing the Gamma distribution. We further propose a novel, efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm for Bayesian inference, designed to be scalable even in high-dimensional settings. We evaluate the method's performance through simulations and apply it to real-world data from the MEG study of a patient with a brain tumor.

We introduce a linear-time decelerator for quantum error correction, capable of processing certain quantum LDPC codes with a constant rate. This decoder operates in $O(n)$ time, where $n$ denotes the code length, and achieves a constant distance of at least $\Omega(n^\alpha)$ for any $\alpha < 1/2$. This result aligns with the time complexity achieved by the belief-deaier approach on quantum LDPC codes, yet it offers a significant advantage by supporting constant-rate codes with arbitrarily long distances under the belief-deaier framework is limited to codes with a vanishing rate. Our methodology relies on a novel application of the belief-deaier approach, which we term "local belief-deaier." In this approach, we approximate the belief messages by considering only a constant number of neighboring qubits, rather than the full set of $O(n)$ qubits. We prove that for a broad category of quantum LDPC codes, this localized approximation is sufficient to guarantee the code's distance and performance under the decoder. Our findings have profound implications for the development of fault-tolerant quantum computers, as they suggest that the belief-deaier approach, which has been limited to codes with a vanishing rate, can be applied to codes with a constant rate. This paper addresses the Distributed Distance-$r$ Dominating Group (DDDG) problem, a novel challenge in distributed computing where a network of nodes must collectively form a specific subset. The objective is to identify a subset $S$ such that every node outside $S$ has at least $r$ neighbors within it, while minimizing the size of $S$. This problem generalizes the well-known distributed dominating group challenge, which corresponds to the case where $r=1$. We examine DDDG within the context of synchronous networks possessing a high girth, operating under the LOCAL model. Our primary contribution is a deterministic algorithm capable of solving DDDG in a synchronous network with a high girth in a time complexity of $O(\log n)$, where $n$ represents the network size. This algorithm relies on a specific graph property termed "distance-$r$ domination number," which is defined as the smallest possible size of such a subset $S$. We further establish that our algorithm's performance is optimal for any sparse network with a high girth, as the resulting subset size matches a lower bound of $n/2 - o(n)$.

This study investigates how disorder affects the bulk and surface states within two-dimensional (2D) higher-order topological insulators (HOTTIs) using a tight-binding model. We demonstrate that the bulk-surface correspondence holds true in such systems despite the presence of disorder. Furthermore, we illustrate that the correspondence between bulk and edge states is maintained even when disorder causes the edge states to merge into the bulk states. Our findings are supported by numerical simulations of the bulk and edge states, as well as calculations of the bulk and surface Chern numbers.

The CMS collaboration at the CERN Large Hadron Collider has conducted an analysis of proton-proton collision data at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, utilizing a dataset corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 137 fb⁻¹ collected during Run 2. This analysis targets supersymmetry (SUSY) scenarios involving the decay of gluinos and first- and second-generation squarks into bottom quarks, neutralinos, and charginos. These decay pathways result in final states characterized by significant missing transverse momentum and varying numbers of jets and leptons. The study employs a combination of multivariate techniques and dedicated control regions to isolate signal from background processes. The resulting limits are expressed as exclusions in the SUSY parameter space, specifically within the context of the phenomenological Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (pMSSM).

We introduce Bright Field Neural Rendering, a novel framework for high-quality, real-time rendering of high-FOV brightfield microscopy. Our method utilizes a neural network to synthesize novel views from a sparse set of reference images, eliminating the need for multiplane or light-sweep acquisitions. This approach enables interactive frame rates while maintaining multiplane resolution, and it supports both static and dynamic samples. Furthermore, Bright Field Neural Rendering significantly reduces motion artifacts caused by live sample movement. The method also demonstrates robustness against illumination inconsistencies and optical aberrations, facilitating the generation of high-fidelity 3D volumes from a minimal number of input frames.

Speckle interferometry is a technique that captures a vast array of short-exposure images to derive precise astrometric data. This study details the findings from a project conducted in 2021 using the 4.1-meter Southern Astrophysical Research (SOAR) telescope at Cerro Tololo, Chile. The primary objective was to measure the separation between the binary star HD 168423, which has an angular separation of 0.2 arcseconds and an orbital period of 11.5 years. The analysis of the collected data yielded a measurement of the projected separation of 100 milliarcseconds, with an uncertainty of 1.5 milliarcseconds. Additionally, the study provides a projected orbital separation of 100 ± 1.5 arcseconds for the binary system HD 168423. We demonstrate that the holographic celestial chiral algebra, which corresponds to the four-dimensional chiral conformal algebra $\mathfrak{g}_c$, can be derived from the four-dimensional color-kinematics duality known as hue-kinematics. This derivation utilizes a specific set of Feynman diagrams featuring a unique interaction vertex. By applying the diagrammatic expansion of $\mathfrak{g}_c$ alongside the principles of integrability, we show that the chiral algebra is equivalent to the quantum affine algebra $A_1^{(1)}$ at a critical quantum parameter.

This study details the analysis of a low-frequency solar radio burst detected by the Low Frequency Array (LOFAR) on 2016 April 13. The event involved a piston-driven shock wave generated by a jet shock, which propagated through a low-density coronal region. The radio burst was localized to a compact source approximately 100 km in size, situated roughly 10 M\textsuperscript{3} above the solar surface. The emission originated from a shock-driven shock drift acceleration mechanism, where electrons were accelerated by the shock front and subsequently emitted radio waves via the cyclotron maser instability. The analysis of the radio burst's temporal and spectral characteristics, alongside observations from the Solar and Heliospheric Imager (S/HI) and the Atmospheric Imaging Imager (AIA), provided a comprehensive view of the dynamics of the jet shock wave and its interaction with the ambient coronal plasma. The study concludes that the radio burst was likely caused by a shock-driven shock drift acceleration mechanism, where electrons were accelerated by the shock front and subsequently emitted radio waves via the cyclotron maser instability. The General Two Higgs Doublet Model (GHDM) extends the Standard Model by incorporating Yukawa couplings that depend on the Higgs vacuum expectation value (VEV). This dependence introduces a new degree of freedom, allowing the model to address flavor anomalies while remaining consistent with existing flavor constraints. In this study, we analyze the likelihood of GHDM by examining the branching ratios for $B_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B \to K^*\mu^+\mu^-$ decays, alongside the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon. Our results indicate that a CP-violating scenario can accommodate the flavor anomalies, whereas a CP-conserving case requires a Higgs sector with at least three doublets.

We introduce a novel functional stochastic differential equation (fSDE) designed to model the statistical behavior of a single vortex within a two-dimensional periodic Navier-Stokes framework. This functional equation extends the standard finite-dimensional SDEs found in literature by accommodating an infinite sequence of stochastic integrals. Our approach derives the vorticity probability law directly from the weak formulation of the Navier-Stokes equations equipped with vorticity as a driving noise. We demonstrate that this constructed measure satisfies the fSDE and establish a unique solution to the equation itself. Furthermore, we outline a constructive algorithm for solving the fSDE and provide a proof of its well-posedness.

We introduce a theoretical framework to examine the evolution of entanglement within the complete state vector of boson sampling as a function of circuit depth. Our findings indicate that, unlike qubit-based quantum circuits, boson sampling generates distinct types of multipartite entanglement that are not merely scaled-up versions of standard bipartite entanglement. We demonstrate that the total state vector of boson sampling can be expressed as a product of two components: one representing a specific form of multipartite entanglement and the other representing multipartileableness. Specifically, the multipartition structure is defined by the permanent of a submatrix of the input transmission matrix, while the multipartitionableness is determined by the reduced transmission matrix. Furthermore, we observe that the rate of entanglement growth in boson sampling circuits is significantly slower than in qubit circuits. These characteristics suggest that the unique properties of boson sampling can be effectively leveraged to develop new methodologies for entanglement generation and control.

We introduce a new method for learning temporal sequences that are both brief and high-dimensional, drawing on data from life science fields. Our approach utilizes a guided variational autoencoder (VAE) to train a latent variable model capable of generating these sequences. The model's architecture comprises a conditional VAE, which creates the data given an input condition, and a variational encoder that learns the posterior distribution of the latent variables. Crucially, the two components are trained together using an auxiliary guidance network. This network is trained on a separate set of data to provide guidance, ensuring the variational encoder produces a tighter approximation of the true posterior distribution. The method was evaluated using two real-world datasets: one consisting of time-lapse images of *Dictyostelium discoideum* cells and another comprising time-series gene expression profiles.

This study investigates the advantages of recurrent networks over feedforward ones in dynamic, partially observable settings. We demonstrate that while recurrent networks can surpass feedforward models in such environments, they may also adopt a suboptimal strategy of relying exclusively on the most recent observation, effectively ignoring their internal history. To analyze this behavior, we examine the conditions under which a rational agent optimizes performance in these domains. We establish that an optimal agent must integrate both their current belief regarding the state and their meta-cognitive assessment of the reliability of that belief. We further illustrate that recurrent networks can successfully approximate these two components, with their internal units representing the agent's beliefs and their gating mechanisms regulating the weight assigned to those beliefs based on the agent's confidence.

Action detection involves identifying the start and end times of actions within a video, as well as locating the specific video segments where these actions occur. While prior research has largely focused on strong supervision, this study addresses the more challenging scenario of weak supervision, where only video-level labels are available. We introduce a novel, end-to-end, weakly-supervised action detection framework that leverages temporal context to enhance performance. Our method utilizes Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) to model the interrelationships between different video segments, enabling the system to identify action regions effectively. Additionally, we have created a new benchmark dataset, known as UCF101 Context, which features high-resolution frames and temporal context data. Experiments demonstrate that our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in weakly-supervised action detection.

The 2021 Image Similarity Challenge (ISC) evaluated methods for detecting duplicate images, a critical capability for applications like visual search, content filtering, and reverse image lookup. Participants were tasked with identifying duplicate pairs within a dataset of 1.2 million images featuring diverse transformations such as color shifts, rotations, and geometric alterations. This year's evaluation notably included a dedicated track for assessing the precision of bounding box localization on duplicated objects. The article details the competition's outcomes, analyzes the top-performing submissions, and introduces a new dataset benchmarking the state-of-the-art in general image similarity tasks.

This work investigates the perturbation of a parabolic differential operator $L$ with a negative leading coefficient, specifically focusing on the associated diffusion process. The analysis covers the spectral properties of $L$ within a bounded domain $\Omega$ subject to boundary conditions, as well as the homogenization of $L$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ under the assumption that the process is transient. Furthermore, the study examines metastability characteristics in scenarios where the process is neither recurrent nor transient.

This study investigates the equation of state for nuclear matter under strong magnetic fields by employing the variational Green's function method within the relativistic mean-field framework. We utilize the Local Occupied Component (LOCV) technique to construct the energy density, incorporating the magnetic field's influence on the energy of the system. The results indicate that the equation of state for nuclear matter in strong magnetic fields is stiffer compared to that in their absence.

Federated learning (FL) offers a privacy-preserving approach to machine learning by keeping data local to clients. However, FL systems face two critical vulnerabilities: they are susceptible to differential privacy (DP) attacks, and the reliance on a central server for secure multi-party computation (SMPC) creates a single point of failure. To address these issues, this paper introduces DP-REC, a novel framework that simultaneously ensures privacy against attacks and improves communication efficiency. By integrating a recursive encryption scheme with a secure comparison protocol, our method eliminates the need for a central server while significantly reducing bandwidth usage. We have implemented a prototype of this framework and evaluated it using a real-world FL scenario. The results demonstrate that our approach achieves a 100-fold reduction in communication costs compared to existing solutions, without compromising the privacy guarantees of the learning process.

The Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer (FUSE) has been employed to observe the Taurus-Perseus-Aquila complex, a region known for its rich star formation activity. The study targets the Lyman-$\alpha$ emission line to map the distribution of neutral hydrogen (HI) across the complex. The analysis reveals a distinct spatial pattern: dense concentrations of HI are found within the Taurus and Perseus molecular clouds, whereas the Aquila region exhibits significantly lower HI density. Furthermore, the study investigates the origins of this emission by examining the relationship between Lyman-$\alpha$ intensity and the column density of molecular hydrogen ($H_2$). The results indicate that Lyman-$\alpha$ is strongly correlated with $H_2$ column density in the Taurus and Perseus clouds, suggesting that the emission is primarily driven by starlight shining through these clouds. In contrast, the low levels of emission in the Aquila region are attributed to the absence of significant $H_2$ column density.

Tables are essential for conveying tabular data in documents, yet extracting this information from PDF files remains difficult. This paper introduces a novel table retrieval framework that leverages Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to generate comprehensive representations for both tables and documents. Our method models a document as a directed graph where nodes represent cells and edges represent relationships between adjacent cells. Similarly, a table is depicted as a graph consisting of cells as nodes and edges linking neighboring cells. By applying the GNN to these structures, we derive robust feature vectors for tables and documents. Experimental results indicate that this approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving an improvement of 10.1% in Mean Average Precision (MAP) on the PubTabSum dataset.

This paper introduces a multi-stage game framework designed to analyze the strategic interactions between a government and a private firm regarding the introduction of new products. In this model, the government determines whether to subsidize a firm's product launch, while the firm decides on the level of research and development (R&D) investment. A key feature is that neither party possesses complete information about the true state of the market; however, the government holds a superior informational advantage compared to the firm. The analysis demonstrates that this informational asymmetry can result in a divergence between the firm's R&D investment and the socially optimal level. Specifically, the firm may either underinvest or overinvest relative to the social optimum. The direction of this deviation is contingent upon the firm's private knowledge of the market state and the magnitude of its informational edge over the government.

This paper outlines the development of a machine learning system designed to estimate population counts in hard-to-reach areas of Mozambique, a nation in southern Africa. The study utilizes data from the 2017 census, which employed autonomous vehicles to capture imagery of nearly 1.2 million residential structures. By integrating this imagery with a dataset of 1.2 million corresponding human-labeled annotations, the authors trained a deep learning model to predict occupancy levels for each dwelling. The results indicate that this automated approach achieves performance comparable to traditional manual counting methods.

Approximate Membership Query (AMQ) filters are essential for efficiently managing large, dynamic sets of data. This paper introduces a novel class of AMQ filters that are false-positive free regarding specific elements while maintaining a controllable false-negative rate. The authors provide a theoretical analysis of the filter's space complexity and describe a practical implementation based on cuckoo filtering. The study evaluates the filter's performance against established approximate algorithms and rigorous exact data structures. The findings indicate that the proposed filter achieves a space efficiency comparable to standard approximate methods and significantly outperforms conventional exact algorithms.

We demonstrate that an all-optical conversion of spinor atoms into molecules is achievable through laser-induced three-body recombination. This mechanism relies on a specific configuration of three interacting energy levels: two metastable states and one excited state. By applying a laser that couples the two metastable states, we can drive the transition of three atoms from this initial configuration to a state comprising two excited atoms and one remaining metastable atom. Subsequently, using a second laser to couple this excited configuration to a final product state consisting of one excited atom and a bound molecule, we facilitate the stable trapping of the resulting molecule. This approach offers a novel pathway for generating ultracold molecules and holds significant potential for advancing quantum simulation and creating specific quantum states.

This study introduces a multi-resolution Smooth Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) approach designed to efficiently handle fluid-structure interactions involving multiple materials. By enabling the use of smaller time steps for specific subsystems, the method optimizes computational resources for large-scale simulations. The framework's efficacy is validated through two benchmark tests: a multi-component free-surface flow scenario and a free-surface flow involving a two-dimensional rigid body.

This paper introduces a novel quantum unsupervised learning algorithm based on the K-Means method, designed for execution on near-term superconducting processors. We detail the specific quantum subroutines required to implement this, including key operations for handling entanglement and measurement. To address the significant overhead of quantum gates, we introduce a quantum-inspired variant that leverages classical computing resources. Furthermore, we outline a quantum-guided learning framework that utilizes a hybrid approach, combining classical and quantum elements to enhance the efficiency of training deep neural networks. We evaluate the proposed methods using both the Iris dataset and a quantum-inspired version of the MNIST dataset. Our results demonstrate that the quantum-inspired algorithm achieves superior performance compared to classical K-Means, while the hybrid quantum-guided learning approach surpasses standard backpropagation in training accuracy.

The FastPitch model is renowned for generating high-quality synthetic speech from pitch contours and phoneme sequences. However, its synthesis quality deteriorates when dealing with specific pitch contours, such as those with low pitch, high pitch variation, or high frequency. This study introduces a pitch augmentation strategy designed to enhance the controllability of FastPitch without compromising speech timbre. By applying a time-scaling technique to the input pitch, we expand its dynamic range, thereby enabling the creation of synthesized audio with lower pitches and greater pitch variability. Experimental results demonstrate that this augmentation technique effectively improves pitch controllability while maintaining superior speech quality.

This paper introduces Hopper, a new multi-hop transformer architecture designed for spatiotemporal inference. Unlike current single-step transformer models, Hopper allows for iterative querying, enabling the system to perform complex, multi-stage reasoning. The framework features a dynamic query mechanism that automatically determines the optimal number of hops required for a given task, balancing performance with computational efficiency. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that Hopper achieves superior results compared to both traditional and state-of-the-art deep learning methods. The codebase is publicly available at https://github.com/lyy99/Hopper.

This study introduces a novel method for determining the mass of the $W$ boson, utilizing a $l^+\ell^-\bar{b}b$ final state. The primary technique involves reconstructing the $W$ boson from the charged lepton, while the bottom quarks are identified through the decay of the associated top quark, which subsequently decays into a $W$ boson and a bottom quark. The other $W$ boson is identified via its hadronic decay. The analysis employs the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider, examining proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV with an integrated luminosity of 139 fb$^{-1}$. The study focuses on events containing an electron or muon, a pair of $b$-jets, and at least one additional jet. The measured mass of the $W$ boson is $80449 \pm 14$ (stat) $\pm 16$ (sys) MeV.

This research investigates how human operators perceive the quality of experience (QoE) when controlling telepresence robots via a 5G network. The study focuses on the influence of latency and bandwidth constraints on task performance and subjective user satisfaction. To address this, we developed a novel QoE model specifically for robot control applications, which incorporates a new metric termed "robot control frustration" to quantify the annoyance caused by network-induced latency. The proposed model was validated through experiments involving 20 participants performing two distinct tasks—a search-and-escape simulation and a treasure hunt—under varying network conditions. The findings indicate that QoE is more sensitive to latency than to available bandwidth, and performance deteriorates more rapidly when the robot is tasked with navigating complex environments.

This paper offers a non-technical introduction to Bayesian hierarchical linear models, designed for researchers and students in the social sciences. It begins by outlining the fundamental concepts of Bayesian inference and then details the construction of linear models, progressing from simple to complex hierarchical structures. The discussion covers the interpretation of model parameters, including fixed and random effects, as well as the use of prior distributions. Furthermore, the text explains how to specify these models using the Stan programming language and interpret their output through posterior distributions and summary statistics. The paper concludes with a practical example applying Bayesian hierarchical linear models to real-world data.

This paper establishes a mathematical model for the Mafia game, a social deduction role-playing activity. The formation of giant planets is a complex process involving the initial formation of a solid core followed by the concurrent accretion of gas from a protoplanetary disk. This study utilizes high-resolution 2D hydrodynamical simulations to examine how two growing giant planets simultaneously draw gas from their shared environment. We explore the impact of this dual accretion on the mass growth of the planets and the structural evolution of the disk. Our findings indicate that the presence of a second planet significantly alters the accretion dynamics of the first, leading to a substantial increase in the first planet's mass growth rate. This acceleration can shorten the time required to reach critical mass by up to 50%. Furthermore, the interaction between the two planets can strip away the outer layers of the disk, causing its total mass to decline by 50% or more. These results demonstrate that the formation of giant planets is a highly interdependent process, where the development of one planet profoundly influences both its own growth and the formation of nearby companions.

Carbon nanotube (CNT) films are promising candidates for flexible electronics, yet their performance is hindered by high contact resistance. While phonon-assisted conduction has been proposed as a potential solution, direct evidence remains elusive. This study presents the first observation of phonon-mediated conduction in an individual armchair CNT, achieved by integrating the nanotube between a metallic gate and a graphene quantum dot (GQD). The GQD functions as a tunable energy filter, allowing researchers to selectively probe phonon-assisted conduction channels. Measurements reveal that conduction current rises exponentially with temperature, a signature of phonon involvement. Furthermore, the specific filtering energy provided by the GQD determines the magnitude of this increase. These findings offer a novel approach for investigating phonon-driven transport in nanoscale systems and provide a pathway to mitigate contact resistance in CNT devices.

Clustering remains a fundamental and extensively researched technique in data mining, particularly for uncovering patterns within unlabeled datasets. However, traditional clustering methods face significant limitations when applied to high-dimensional data, primarily due to the "curse of dimensionality," which causes them to perform poorly. To address this, numerous advanced strategies have been developed to mitigate these dimensional challenges. This paper introduces a novel fuzzy clustering method designed specifically for high-dimensional environments. The proposed approach employs a variable feature weighting mechanism to dynamically adjust feature importance during the clustering process, thereby reducing dimensionality. Furthermore, the objective function is enhanced by incorporating an entropy-based term that refines cluster quality. The study includes a theoretical analysis of the algorithm's convergence and experimental validation across both synthetic and real-world datasets. The results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in clustering high-dimensional data.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become a cornerstone of deep learning, driving significant advancements in areas like natural language processing and computer vision. Despite this widespread adoption, theoretical understanding of their learning remains limited. This paper addresses the gap by analyzing MoEs with linear experts and polynomial activation functions, establishing sample-efficient and statistically consistent gradient descent algorithms. We demonstrate that these properties hold for both homogeneous models, where all experts share the same activation, and heterogeneous models featuring distinct functions. Our approach relies on a novel methodology that transforms the MoE into an equivalent representation involving a mixture of polynomial feature vectors, which we then analyze using techniques from the literature on mixture-of-experts with polynomial experts.

This paper investigates chip-firing games on directed graphs, with a specific emphasis on those that are both balanced and bipartite. Our findings generalize the seminal work of Baker and Norine concerning the Jacobian of such graphs. We demonstrate that for any directed graph exhibiting these properties, every top-type chip-firing configuration results in a divisor whose degree is minimized within its linear equivalence class. This observation leads to the identification of a Jacobian subgroup characterized by the property that its elements possess canonical representatives with non-negative residues at every vertex located within one graph partition set. We establish that the degree of this subgroup corresponds to the size of the relevant partition. Furthermore, we prove that for every top-type divisor, there exists a corresponding top-type divisor within the same equivalence class where the degree is maximized, with elements in this maximal class possessing canonical representatives featuring at most one negative residue. We also show that the size of this maximal subgroup equals that of the original subgroup. Additionally, we prove that when the graph is connected, the union of the two subgroups—representing top-type divisors with non-negative and minimally negative residues, respectively—constitutes the entire Jacobian. Finally, we demonstrate that the intersection of these two subgroups forms a Prym type subgroup, providing an explicit characterization of its size.

Double refraction in the cosmic microwave background (CMB) offers a means to test the CMB's propagation, specifically looking for birefringence that could indicate a broken global symmetry. This study establishes an upper limit on the magnitude of such symmetry breaking within quantum gravity models, derived from the lack of observed birefringence in the CMB. The analysis incorporates a theoretical framework where gravity breaks a global symmetry, leading to CMB birefringence, and applies CMB data to constrain the model parameters. The resulting bounds are competitive with other methods, surpassing limits from gravitational waves and photon dispersion, and are expected to improve with future datasets.

This study utilizes data from the Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope (UVIT) aboard the AstroSat satellite to examine ultraviolet bright stars in the globular cluster NGC 4147. The cluster's fundamental parameters were derived by fitting the observed optical color-magnitude diagram with theoretical isochrones, yielding an age of 11.9 Gyr and a metallicity of $[Fe/H] = -0.85$. The analysis identified 11 UV bright stars, with 6 of them showing variability. The observed variability periods range from 1.1 to 10.1 days, and the amplitude of flux variation in the UVIT FUV band spans 0.01 to 0.1 magnitudes. The study also presents the first UVIT observations of the eclipsing binary system in NGC 4147, NGC 4147V1.

The $M$-module within the stable homotopy ring of types, denoted as $\pi_*(\mathcal{S})$, is generated by elements $b_{k}$ for $k \geq 0$. This result, referred to as the "fragile $b$-principle," is established by demonstrating that the image of the J-homomorphism constitutes the submodule of $\mathcal{S}$'s stable homotopy ring generated by the even-dimensional elements $b_{2k}$.

The transferability of deep learning models is commonly explained by the concept of "two agreements": the alignment between source and target feature representations, and the compatibility between source and target label functions. However, this study challenges the validity of both agreements. Through a theoretical examination of the Bayes optimal classifier, we demonstrate that neither agreement is strictly required for transferring knowledge from source to target domains. Furthermore, we illustrate that these two agreements are not absolute; they are instead contingent upon the specific source and target domains involved. Consequently, we propose a refined framework for understanding model transferability in deep learning.

We investigate how network structure influences the spread of information, specifically examining the relationship between modularity and diffusion velocity. Our findings indicate that information travels faster in networks with lower modularity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this relationship is non-linear, meaning that as modularity increases, diffusion velocity initially drops sharply before stabilizing. Our analysis reveals that this counterintuitive trend arises because highly modular networks concentrate information flow within specific subgroups, thereby restricting its movement across the broader system. These insights offer valuable guidance for designing effective communication strategies aimed at rapidly disseminating information.

We introduce a concept of distinctiveness for Riemann surfaces based on quantitative distance metrics. This framework enables the demonstration that within the Teichmüller space of a hyperbolic surface, the moduli space representing the modularity of the minimal isoperimetric inequality forms the core region of the space, thereby confirming the Thomas-Yau conjecture for the minimal inequality. This result is achieved by proving the moduli space's central location through the application of the quantitative version established here.

The regular perturbation model (RPM) is a widely used analytical approach for estimating the mean and mean-squared error (MSE) of discrete-time nonlinear systems, such as digital communication links. Originally formulated for continuous time, this paper extends the RPM to unamplified discrete-time systems. We demonstrate that the discrete-time RPM (DT-RPM) offers a computationally efficient method for calculating the mean and MSE of unamplified link performance. Furthermore, we establish that the DT-RPM is a valid approximation for both binary phase-shift keying (BPSK) and quadrature phase-shift keying (QPSK) systems.

Mobile devices have become a daily necessity for billions, serving as primary gateways to online platforms and digital services. Consequently, the volume of data collected by these applications has surged, raising significant privacy concerns. While app developers strive to safeguard user information, malicious apps frequently exploit user trust to harvest sensitive data. To address this, researchers have developed various security mechanisms to detect and block such apps. However, evasion attacks have emerged as a critical challenge, enabling malicious apps to bypass detection and continue harvesting data undetected. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of evasion techniques within the Android operating system, categorizing them into three main types: obfuscation, issue-space evasion, and runtime evasion. The survey examines the specific evasion methods, their operational principles, and associated challenges. Furthermore, it outlines future research directions and outlines promising avenues for future study.

Distributed systems are essential for modern applications, yet their management remains difficult due to the need for complex orchestration. While Kubernetes has become a standard solution, it suffers from a steep learning curve and rigid architecture that limits its applicability to specific workloads. This paper introduces Ozy, a new orchestration framework designed to overcome these limitations through a universal container approach. Unlike Kubernetes, Ozy offers a streamlined interface and supports diverse execution environments, including bare metal, virtual machines, and serverless platforms. This paper details Ozy's architecture, implementation, and evaluation, demonstrating that it achieves performance comparable to leading systems while offering greater flexibility and ease of use.

We investigate the ground state of the $\nu=5/2$ quantum Hall phase by employing a variational wave function that accounts for Landau level mixing. Our findings indicate that the state remains stable up to mixing strengths of approximately 10%, a level of coupling where the conventional Pfaffian wave function is known to break down. Furthermore, the energy gap associated with the state exhibits a minimum near a 5% mixing strength, suggesting a potential experimental signature.

The recent work by Berti et al. (2021) posits that the Thakurta metric depicts black holes in cosmological spacetime, a model they argue could explain the gravitational wave signals detected by LIGO and Virgo from binary mergers. This paper challenges that assertion, demonstrating that the Thakurta solution fails to represent black hole mergers within a cosmological framework. We further illustrate that the Thakurta metric does not describe a vacuum spacetime surrounding a black hole; rather, it corresponds to a massive object immersed in a cosmological fluid. Consequently, the constraints on the abundance of Primordial Black Holes (PBHs) derived from LIGO and Virgo observations remain unaffected by this metric analysis.

This study investigates planet formation via pebble accretion within a turbulent protoplanetary disk, specifically examining how gas density fluctuations influence the growth of a growing protoplanet. We employ a 2D local simulation framework that models the accretion process while accounting for variations in the gas surface density. Our results indicate that while gas density fluctuations exert a minor impact on the mean accretion rate, they significantly alter the stochastic nature of growth, thereby shaping the final mass distribution of the resulting protoplanet.

This study examines the learning of noisy parity functions within the class of parity threshold gates (PTGs). A PTG is defined as a linear threshold gate that applies weights exclusively to a subset of parity functions. The authors establish that, given a limited number of training examples, the only PTGs capable of shadily achieving low empirical error utilize exclusively individual single-term parities. Consequently, this finding demonstrates an inability to efficiently learn such restricted gates, as they remain outside the parity hypothesis class. In contrast, when an ample supply of examples is available, these limited-capacity gates become learnable. The authors further prove that, in the presence of noise, any PTG with bounded VC dimension can be efficiently learned. These results are significant because they offer a rare theoretical framework for learning non-linear threshold gates under noisy conditions.
