The Spectral Koopman framework represents a highly effective approach for analyzing nonlinear dynamical systems. Nevertheless, its application is often hindered by the "curse of dimensionality," which causes computational costs to escalate rapidly with increasing system dimensions. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a novel Sparse-Grid-Driven Adaptive Spectral Koopman (SGDASpK) method. This method integrates the benefits of sparse grids and adaptive basis functions to substantially lower both the system's dimensionality and the scaling rate associated with higher dimensions. Furthermore, the proposed SGDASpK method is validated through a series of numerical experiments.

This study introduces a novel outer complex scaling (OCS) approach designed to investigate ionization dynamics in both atoms and molecules subjected to intense direct current electric fields. The methodology involves separating the molecular system's wave function into two components: an inner region, solved using standard real-space techniques, and an outer region, resolved via the complex scaling approach. To facilitate this separation, a multipole expansion is applied to the electric potential within the inner domain. The two regions are subsequently linked by enforcing continuity of both the wave function and its derivative at the interface boundary. The accuracy of the proposed OCS framework is validated by benchmarking its calculated autoionization resonances against those derived from a full complex scaling implementation. Furthermore, the study examines the time evolution of wave packets within the complex plane to analyze the system's temporal behavior.

The Sinkhorn algorithm is a standard iterative method for solving the Schr\"odinger issue, a variant of optimal transport that incorporates independent prior distributions for each marginal. Although the algorithm is guaranteed to converge to the optimal transport plan when independent prior distributions yield a valid solution, it was previously unknown whether it converges when such a solution does not exist. This paper establishes that the algorithm indeed converges in this scenario as well. The proof relies on a novel variational characterization of the optimal transport cost, which demonstrates that the optimal cost is the limit inferior of the algorithm's iterates.

The cross-section for top-antitop quark production has been measured using proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV, recorded by the ATLAS detector at the LHC during 2012. The analysis leverages an integrated luminosity of 2.0 fb$^{-1}$ and selects events via the dilepton decay channel of top quarks. The differential cross-sections are measured as functions of the invariant mass of the dilepton system, the transverse momentum of top quarks, and the pseudorapidity of top quarks. The total inclusive cross-section is determined to be $\sigma_{t\bar{t}} = 7.51 \pm 0.17 \text{(stat)} \pm 0.16 \text{(syst)} \pm 0.11 \text{(lumi)}$ pb. This result aligns with theoretical predictions from next-to-next-to-leading-order calculations in quantum chromodynamics.

We examine a system of $N$ quantum harmonic oscillators subject to a uniform transverse magnetic field and linear coupling, with a single central oscillator coupled nonlinearly to a thermal bath. While the system's eigenstates possess delocalized character, the long-time asymptotic behavior of the excited state populations exhibits distinct properties. We demonstrate that the excitation probability for the central oscillator converges to a constant value, whereas the excitation probabilities for all other oscillators vanish as $1/N$ in the thermodynamic limit. Consequently, the central oscillator remains excited while the remainder of the system becomes fully depleted.

This paper introduces a new generalization of the classical Janowski q-Clarkson inequality using generalized Bessel functions. We establish the sharp bounds for new classes of univalent functions derived from this new framework. Additionally, we investigate key geometric properties of these newly defined function classes.

The pandemic has drastically changed human interactions, yet the specific effects of behavioral shifts on the diversity of urban social encounters remain unclear. By analyzing mobile phone data from 1.2 million individuals in Wuhan, we observed that while the distribution of daily activities became more diverse during the pandemic, the variety of interpersonal meetings actually decreased. This reduction in diversity was more pronounced among the elderly and the young, and persisted longer in this demographic. Furthermore, these encounters exhibited greater homogeneity regarding the income levels of participants. These findings suggest that pandemic-induced restrictions disproportionately limited access to diverse social networks for vulnerable groups, potentially exacerbating existing social and economic inequalities.

This study evaluates several field-splitting strategies designed to address the nonlinear challenges inherent in simulating two-phase flow through heterogeneous porous media. The proposed splits are designed to decouple the strongly nonlinear constitutive relationships—specifically relative permeability and capillary pressure—from the linear transport operators, thereby enhancing the efficiency of black-oil reservoir simulators. The analysis examines how various methods handle capillary pressure and relative permeability, with specific attention to the influence of grid resolution and the statistical characteristics of the porous medium. The findings indicate that while the specific splitting approach has minimal impact on the simulation's convergence rate, it significantly impacts computational cost.

We introduce a new category of optical resonators that are intrinsically chiral, meaning they favor the interaction with either left- or right-handed circularly polarized light. This unique property arises from a non-local interaction between polarization and orbital angular momentum, a mechanism that can be engineered using metasurfaces. This work outlines the theoretical framework for these chisral resonators, describes their distinctive polarization-dependent characteristics, and explores their potential applications in the selective excitation of chiral molecules.

We demonstrate that the JT gravitational limit of Liouville CFT is defined by a $U(N)$ matrix model featuring a potential that scales as $O(N)$. This construction aligns with the $U(N)$ matrix model proposed in arXiv:2205.08607, which describes the holographic dual of JT gravity on a hyperbolic disk. Our findings indicate that the boundary cosmological constant in the dual matrix model corresponds to the dressing charge in the CFT, while the hyperbolic background geometry of the disk emerges from a specific profile of the matrix model potential.

This study examines the Alcubierre metric within a perfect fluid framework incorporating a cosmological constant ($\Lambda$). We demonstrate that a $\Lambda$-term can offset the negative energy density required by Alcubierre's original warp drive proposal, thereby enabling solutions for both subluminal speeds ($v_s < c$) and superluminal speeds ($v_s > c$). For subluminal drives, we identify two distinct perfect fluid solutions: one representing dust and another representing a perfect fluid. In contrast, superluminal speed scenarios yield solutions only for a perfect fluid.

The GUIDES project, supported by the European Commission's Horizon 2020 programme, aims to develop a comprehensive framework for a new generation of geospatial information systems tailored for urban infrastructure. This framework will facilitate the integration of diverse data sources, including traditional 2D/3D GIS, Building Information Models (BIM), and Internet of Things (IoT) data. The project's primary objective is to create a unified, multi-disciplinary digital representation of urban infrastructure that enhances data accessibility and interoperability. By leveraging advanced technologies such as semantic web standards, machine learning, and data fusion, GUIDES seeks to enable intelligent analysis and the automated generation of new insights. Ultimately, the project intends to deliver a flexible, modular, and open-source solution designed for application across various urban infrastructure domains.

We introduce a novel method for characterizing the motional state distribution of a trapped ion, leveraging spin dephasing induced by coupling between the ion's internal spin and its vibrational modes. This approach offers a sensitive tool for investigating the dynamical processes that populate ion motional states. We have applied this method to examine the heating mechanisms affecting a single $^{40}\text{Ca}^+$ ion, confirming that heating arises from ion collisions with background gas. Furthermore, we utilized this technique to measure the ion's heating rate, the temperature of its vibrational modes, and the ion's collision velocity with the background gas.

This study investigates the chemical enhancement effect in Tip-Enhanced Raman Scattering (TERS) by examining the interaction between a silver nanoparticle and a benzene molecule using a quantum mechanical approach. By employing density functional theory (DFT) to calculate the electronic structures of these systems, we derived the scattering cross-sections for incident electromagnetic waves. Subsequently, we applied time-dependent electromagnetic theory to compute the Raman scattering intensity arising from molecular polarizability. Our results indicate that the chemical enhancement effect is negligible compared to local field enhancement. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the anisotropic polarizability tensor of the molecule is the primary driver of the TERS signal, with the local field enhancement effect playing a secondary role.

We report non-detections of anomalous radio emission in the nearby galaxy cluster, utilizing K-band observations from the Sardinia Radio Telescope (SRT). The study targets a sample of 100 galaxies with redshifts $z < 0.01$ and absolute magnitudes $M_r < -18$ mag, selected from the SDSS DR10 catalog. The primary objective is to identify potential sources of non-thermal radio emission that deviates from standard stellar populations. The analysis involved obtaining spectra for 100 of these objects and calculating their radio flux densities at 1.4 GHz. The resulting upper limits on non-thermal emission are generally consistent with previous findings, though they are notably tighter for the brightest galaxies.

The discovery of extensive entropy change in molecular caloric materials like $(NH_4)_2SO_4$ has prompted a re-examination of their underlying mechanisms. This study employs first-principles calculations to analyze the electronic and vibrational characteristics of the ammonium ion within the crystal lattice. Our findings indicate that the entropy change stems from the vibrational modes of the ion, specifically involving a transition from a two-dimensional to a three-dimensional harmonic potential well. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the resulting entropy change is independent of the specific potential well shape, relying instead on the transition dimensionality.

Reinforcement learning (RL) theories describe how the brain learns to maximize future rewards by integrating prior knowledge with new information signaled by dopamine-driven prediction errors. Although these theories predict a specific, optimal policy, real-world behavior often deviates from perfection. This study investigates whether such deviations are random or if they reflect consistent, individual-specific strategies. By analyzing choices from 100 participants in a sequential decision-making task, we identified two suboptimal patterns: a tendency to over-explore and a propensity for perseveration. These tendencies were found to be trait-like, meaning they remained stable across different tasks and were significantly correlated with one another. Furthermore, the neural encoding of prediction errors in the midbrain varied based on these individual traits, suggesting that the magnitude of dopaminergic responses is influenced by a person's specific exploratory or perseveratory tendencies.

We introduce a $E_8$ core architecture designed to model quantum entanglement and contextuality within a $2^{16}-1$ dimensional Hilbert space. This framework utilizes the complexification of a real $E_8$ core, where the real core consists of 240 vectors in an 8-dimensional real Hilbert space. These vectors are organized into 16 groups of 15, with each set forming a basis for the real space. The complexification expands this to a 256-dimensional space, which is then embedded into a 2$^{16}-1$-dimensional Hilbert space. This embedding is achieved by associating each basis vector with a specific qubit state. The resulting 2$^{16}-1$-dimensional space accommodates 65,535 basis vectors, each representing a unique state. This architecture provides a theoretical foundation for investigating quantum entanglement and contextuality within the $E_8$ core system.

We introduce a novel framework for time series similarity search based on the Fréchet distance, a metric that effectively captures both shape and size variations. Although recent advances have achieved near-linear time exact Fréchet Close Neighbor Search (CNS), practical applications demand faster approximate solutions. We present a new approximate Fréchet CNS algorithm that offers a provable trade-off between query time and approximation quality. Our method improves upon the prior best bound by reducing the query time exponent from 0.75 to 0.625, yielding a substantial performance gain. Additionally, we establish lower bounds on query time for approximate Fréchet CNS, demonstrating that our upper bounds are tight up to constant factors.

Measurement inaccuracies in noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices severely hinder the ability to gather meaningful data for large-scale computations. While prior research has proposed various error correction methods, they often demand extensive resources or rely on assumptions that may not hold true in practice. This work introduces a novel, scalable approach to correcting measurement faults by applying iterative Bayesian unfolding to raw readout data. The method is supported by a rigorous theoretical framework that establishes its convergence and demonstrates its efficacy through numerical simulations. The study also explores the implementation of this technique on actual NISQ hardware, highlighting its potential for scaling up to systems comprising thousands of qubits.

Shared autonomy represents a critical research domain within robotics, focusing on transferring control from a human operator to a robot. This transition is essential for enabling robots to function effectively in unstructured settings where human presence is required. A significant challenge in this field is the difficulty of modeling human intent, particularly when a human's goals are not explicitly defined. This paper introduces a new methodology for inferring human intent by leveraging human knowledge of the robot's physical capabilities. The study validates this approach using a physical simulation involving a differential-drive robot tasked with reaching a specific target. The results indicate that the proposed method outperforms baseline techniques in accuracy. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that shared autonomy frameworks can serve as an effective mechanism for communication between humans and robots, allowing people to convey their objectives through physical actions.

This paper introduces HiTMap, a novel hierarchical topological map designed to facilitate navigation within unknown domains. The proposed architecture consists of a hierarchical structure where a coarse-level map is constructed first, followed by the incremental generation of finer levels of detail as exploration proceeds. Experimental results demonstrate that HiTMap achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both computational efficiency and memory usage.

This paper introduces a novel method for building inter-group complementary code sets (ICCS) and two-dimensional (2-D) zero side-lobe supplementary array code sets (ZSACS) utilizing multivariable functions. The proposed ICCS construction method achieves a larger size and a longer processing gain compared to existing ICCS types. Furthermore, the new 2-D ZSACS construction approach results in a higher code size and a greater processing gain than current 2-D generalized array codes (2-D GACs) used for zero side-lobe applications.

X-ray computed tomography (CT) is a medical imaging technique that reconstructs a 3D representation of a subject's internal structure from multiple 2D projections acquired at varying energy levels. This paper introduces a novel variational framework designed to simultaneously reconstruct a polyenergetic CT volume, denoise the raw sensor data, and decompose the materials within the subject. By leveraging the inherent sparsity of the underlying image and the non-convexity of the noise model, our approach achieves superior denoising and material decomposition accuracy compared to existing methods. The resulting optimization problem is addressed using an alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) scheme, which is further enhanced with a fast, differentiable, and accurate implementation of the probability-based noise model. Experimental evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets confirm the framework's effectiveness.

The interaction between a metallic surface and a dielectric interface, combined with the influence of electron spill-out and nonlocal effects, can alter the characteristics of gap-plasmons. This study investigates the dispersion relations of gap-plasmons in the limiting case where the gap approaches zero, specifically examining how these factors affect the system. The analysis demonstrates that while the dispersion relation remains largely independent of the gap size under these conditions, the group velocity is significantly modified by the electron spill-out and nonlocal effects. The study further explores the influence of the dielectric constant on gap size, revealing that increasing the dielectric constant leads to a reduction in the nonlocal correction to the group velocity. Additionally, it is observed that the electron spill-out effect consistently reduces the group velocity, regardless of variations in the dielectric constant.

We introduce a new method for extracting named entities from documents based on specific queries. This approach employs a query-expanded context, generated using a topic model, to facilitate entity identification. The system integrates contextual information with term relevance to produce a refined query-expanded context, which is subsequently matched against named entities to calculate their contextual relevance scores. The study evaluates two distinct models for determining contextual importance: the first relies on a fixed distribution of context words, while the second utilizes a dynamic distribution derived from the specific query. The proposed algorithm demonstrates superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques across various benchmarks.

Time series data is frequently characterized by high dimensionality, encompassing numerous variables, time points, and data series. While current visualization tools often struggle to effectively support the exploration of such complex datasets, this paper introduces a novel approach to display multivariate time series data. Our method visualizes all series within a single view, utilizing a two-dimensional layout to encode additional variables. We have developed a set of interaction techniques that facilitate both overview generation and deep data exploration. Furthermore, we conducted an empirical study to evaluate these interactions, and our findings indicate that they successfully enable users to identify both common and unique patterns across the data series.

Although Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have proven effective for modeling relational data, they typically require a uniform node representation, which is often unattainable in real-world scenarios where entities possess diverse attributes. To address this, we introduce Heterogeneous Resemblance GNNs (HRGNNs), a new architecture designed to handle such varied data types. Our method employs a novel "resemblance" mechanism that captures both intra-group and inter-group similarities between nodes of different types. Experimental evaluations on three real-world datasets drawn from the MIMIC-III database demonstrate that HRGNNs significantly outperform existing methods in handling heterogeneous attributes. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the model effectively captures both internal and cross-type similarities, thereby offering a robust solution for complex real-life data modeling.

This study examines the influence of solvent polarization on the charge distribution within an electric double layer adjacent to a hard, charged, and soft interface within an electrolyte solution. We introduce a new theoretical framework that integrates the Poisson equation with a modified Poisson-Boltzmann equation to account for polarization effects. Our analysis reveals that while the electric field intensity within the double layer remains largely unaffected by solvent polarization, the overall potential drops significantly. This reduction leads to a diminished surface charge density and a compressed double layer. Furthermore, we observe that polarization suppresses the size of the brush layer formed by the grafted chains. These findings are validated against our results using Monte Carlo simulations.

This paper introduces a method for identifying software specifications within unformatted documents, such as emails, memos, and documentation. Specifications are defined as descriptions of desired system behaviors, including functional and non-functional requirements, usage scenarios, and system constraints. The proposed approach employs a two-stage process: initially, it detects specification sentences by leveraging syntactic cues, and subsequently, it refines these candidates using semantic features. The study evaluates the system on the SPECs dataset, which contains annotated specifications from 1,000 documents. The results demonstrate that the suggested technique outperforms existing methods.

This study addresses the optimization of end-to-end network energy consumption in multi-hop networks by jointly scheduling relays and allocating transmit power. The multi-objective problem is formulated as a mixed-integer non-linear programming (MINLP) model. To solve this, we first derive a closed-form expression for the optimal continuous power distribution under a fixed relay schedule. Subsequently, we transform the original MINLP into a binary linear programming problem by approximating the non-linear energy function using a piecewise linear approach. The resulting formulation is resolved via the column-and-constraint generation method, which yields an optimal relay schedule and corresponding power levels. Simulation outcomes confirm that this proposed scheme achieves superior energy efficiency compared to existing benchmarks.

This study presents a first-principles relativistic theory of Yu-Shiba-Rusinov (YSR) states, utilizing a Green's function approach that incorporates the self-energy of a magnetic impurity alongside the non-magnetic substrate's Green's function. We applied this framework to investigate the YSR states of a single Mn atom and various Mn clusters deposited on a Nb(110) surface. Our analysis reveals that the non-local spin-orbit coupling (SOc) of Nb is the primary driver of the splitting observed in the Mn-induced YSR states. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the degree of spin-orbit coupling in Nb is the critical factor determining the splitting of these states.

The study reports the initial investigation into the rare decay mode $K^+\to\pi^+\nu\bar{\nu}$ utilizing the decay-in-motion approach with the NA62 experiment at CERN. This analysis examines 1.01 billion kaons, of which 1.01 billion were observed. This study introduces a distribution-to-distribution (D2D) scan matching approach designed to counteract biases inherent in conventional methods. While standard techniques typically rely on matching probability density functions (PDFs) between corresponding segments of two scans, this new approach utilizes deep neural networks (DNNs) to learn a mapping function that aligns the scans. The proposed D2D method was evaluated against the widely used cross-correlation (CC) algorithm using both simulated and real-world data. The results demonstrate that the D2D approach achieves superior accuracy compared to the standard cross-correlation method.

Satellite imagery serves as a vital resource for monitoring the environment, detecting changes, and supporting disaster relief efforts. While numerous studies have leveraged deep learning for image analysis, these methods often demand extensive computational resources and large datasets. This paper introduces a novel, non-deep-learning approach for edge detection in satellite photos, utilizing a convolutional neural network (CNN) for feature extraction. The proposed method relies on a single, optimized network that minimizes the need for training data and computational overhead. Experimental results indicate that this technique achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art deep learning models.

Non-linear X-ray absorption near-edge spectroscopy (NIXANES) has emerged as a powerful tool for investigating electronic transitions in materials, particularly those exhibiting strong electron-electron and spin-orbit interactions. This study introduces a rate-based theoretical framework that models NIXANES spectra by accounting for the temporal evolution of core-excited electron groups. The theory employs a generalized x-ray absorption cross-section formula, which incorporates the time-dependent wave function of excited electron groups. The theory's validity is demonstrated by successfully reproducing NIXANES spectra of O 1s in CO₂ and N 1s in N₂, calculated using the GW approximation to determine core-excited electron group energies.

This paper introduces a generator-based approach designed to enhance the robustness of modulation classification against adversarial attacks. While machine learning has significantly improved classification accuracy, it remains highly vulnerable to these attacks, which introduce minimal, imperceptible perturbations to cause misclassification. To address this, we propose utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to generate adversarial examples that aid in training more resilient models. Specifically, we developed a new GAN architecture that produces both clean and adversarial inputs, thereby boosting the resilience of the resulting classifier. Our experimental results demonstrate that this approach yields a 10% improvement in accuracy when evaluated on an additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel.

Segmentation of brain lesions in multiple sclerosis (MS) is a critical clinical task, yet it remains labor-intensive. Deep learning has emerged as a promising solution, yet the availability of large-scale annotated datasets is scarce. While transfer learning is often employed to mitigate this issue, the extent to which it improves performance in medical imaging remains uncertain. This study evaluates transfer learning for T1-weighted MRI lesion segmentation by comparing models trained continuously against those trained from scratch. Using data from three hospitals, the research assesses performance across both cross-institutional and intra-institutional settings. Findings indicate that models trained continuously outperform those trained from scratch in both scenarios, achieving Dice scores of 0.655 and 0.680, respectively. Furthermore, continuous training demonstrates superior scalability; it yields higher gains in the challenging cross-institutional setting compared to the easier intra-institutional one, whereas a model trained from scratch shows relatively consistent performance across both environments.

We introduce a novel technique for generating high-contrast, high-resolution images of binary stars, leveraging the natural orbital motion of the pair. By utilizing a reference image captured at a different orbital phase, the method isolates the target system from the static background through the subtraction of scaled versions of the reference. We demonstrate that this approach yields superior contrast compared to standard speckle interferometry, enabling the detection of faint companions near bright primaries. The technique is validated using observations of the star HD 142529, revealing a companion with a magnitude difference of 4.5 and an angular separation of 0.12 arcseconds.

This study introduces a theoretical framework for analyzing how machine learning models for dynamical systems can fail. We define a "model error metric" to quantify the discrepancy between a true system and its approximation, demonstrating that the evolution of this error is governed by a time-dependent model complexity and a stability function derived from the underlying dynamics. This formulation enables the investigation of how dynamical properties influence model performance. Specifically, we illustrate that while simple attractors like points and lines are straightforward to replicate, replicating more intricate structures, such as chaotic attractors, poses significant challenges. Furthermore, we show that the model error can be amplified by the dynamical system's Lyapunov exponents, which quantify sensitivity to initial conditions. These theoretical insights are validated through experiments applying a neural network to replicate both the Lorenz and Rössler attractors.

The formation of massive stars is a critical yet unresolved issue in astrophysics. While it is generally accepted that these stars originate within dense cores, the specific mechanisms driving their creation remain elusive. This study investigates the core of the infrared dark cloud Dragon, a region hosting a massive star-forming complex. We utilized high-resolution data from the Herschel Space Observatory to analyze the physical and chemical properties of the core's densest part. Our findings reveal a core with a mass of 1,000 solar masses and a radius of 0.14 parsecs, characterized by a central expansion at a velocity of 0.06 parsecs per million years. This expansion is hypothesized to result from the outflows of a massive protostar. Additionally, we identified a central cavity with a radius of 0.01 parsecs, likely created by the protostar's wind or jet activity. These observations support a model where core expansion, driven by a massive outflow, facilitates the collapse of surrounding material, thereby enabling the formation of massive stars.

Primordial black holes (PBHs) constitute a compelling candidate for dark matter, and the PopSyCLE framework offers a robust method for simulating their evolution. This study details the integration of PBH formation and early cosmological dynamics into PopSyCLE, enabling the calculation of abundance for various formation scenarios. We examine the impact of the early matter-dominated era on PBH formation, specifically analyzing how the duration of this era influences the PBH mass distribution. Additionally, we explore PBH formation mechanisms arising from the collapse of curvature perturbations, utilizing a power spectrum derived from inflationary models. We further investigate the constraints on PBH abundance imposed by microlensing observations, particularly from the OGLE survey, and discuss how these limits vary with the fraction of dark matter accounted for by PBHs.

This study examines the behavior of hard wedge particles modeled as half spheres joined at their flat faces. Our findings reveal that these particles exhibit a nematic phase characterized by splay modulation, where the splay parameter is determined by the aspect ratio of the constituent spheres. Additionally, we report a smectic phase featuring splay-modulated layers. The stability of this phase is contingent upon the particle density and the splay parameter. Our results align with the theoretical framework of modulated phases, specifically the modulated nematic and modulated smectic phases described by the Beresinskii-Lebowitz model.

Parameter-efficient tuning (PEt) has recently emerged as a cost-effective alternative to full fine-tuning, enabling the adaptation of pre-trained models through the adjustment of a minimal number of parameters. This work introduces a novel PEt technique, Special Token Adaptation (STA), which modifies the embeddings of specific tokens within the model's hidden layer. We demonstrate that STA can be seamlessly integrated with various existing PEt methods, resulting in improved performance. Empirical evaluations on multiple NLP tasks, including GLUE, CoQA, and SQuAD, reveal that STA achieves performance on par with full fine-tuning while utilizing only 0.0001% of the model's total parameters.

This paper investigates the extension of a given set of alternatives by analyzing how individuals rank collections of options. We introduce two distinct methods for these set-based preference orderings: the first is non-contextual, meaning the comparison between any two sets remains consistent regardless of other available alternatives; the second is contextual, meaning a pair of sets may be preferred differently depending on the broader context of available choices. We demonstrate that non-contextual orderings can be modeled using a probability distribution over individual preferences over the alternatives, whereas contextual orderings arise from distributions over distributions over those alternatives. We also establish that contextual preference structures offer greater expressive power than their non-contextual counterparts. Finally, we illustrate how both types of preferences can be learned from data and compare their performance on a synthetic dataset.

This study investigates the connections between dynamic and thermodynamic characteristics in a low molecular mass ($M_w = 2,000$ g/mol) glass-former, poly(2-methyl-2-oxazoline) (P(MMA)). Utilizing differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), dielectric spectroscopy, and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), researchers examined how temperature and frequency influence the glass transition and structural relaxation. The findings indicate that the dielectric relaxation response and NMR spin-lattice relaxation time ($T_1$) are governed by the same effective activation energy, which correlates with the temperature-dependent segmental enthalpy derived from DSC. Consequently, the primary factor driving the slowing of structural relaxation in the glass region is the thermodynamic state of the system.

This study investigates the rejection of inappropriate responses during language model training, hypothesizing that such rejection is a critical factor in achieving high-quality performance. We introduce a new training approach called Rejection Augmented Pretraining (RAP), which leverages this mechanism. By generating multiple outputs for each input and having a rejections classifier identify and remove those of lower quality, RAP effectively discards subpar generations. Our experiments on the C4 dataset demonstrate that this method yields a 0.2 improvement in perplexity compared to standard transformer models. Additionally, we analyze the rejection classifier, offering insights into how language models process and identify invalid language.

Current neural machine translation (NMT) models typically rely on the previous token to generate the current one, a strategy that can result in suboptimal outputs. This study introduces a new look-ahead focus mechanism designed to enhance generation quality by enabling the model to attend to future tokens. The approach utilizes an auxiliary decoder that predicts the primary decoder's hidden states based on future input, allowing the primary decoder to integrate this information into its generation process. Evaluated on the WMT 2014 English-German and English-French newstest2014 test sets, the model achieved a 0.20 BLEU improvement over the baseline on English-German and a 0.19 BLEU improvement on English-French. We calculate the Kontsevich weights for graphs representing connections and curvatures within symplectic manifolds equipped with a Poisson structure. These explicit computations demonstrate that the Wess-Zumino-Witten (ZW) model associated with a symplectic manifold and its corresponding graph representation is equivalent to the model of a line bundle equipped with a connection and curvature, where the curvature is determined by the Poisson tensor. This result confirms a conjecture proposed by Witten.

We investigate large-$N$ conformal field theories (CFTs) with large central charges that possess a dual description via large-$\lambda$ string theory or supergravity. By analyzing the information contained in thermal and entanglement entropies, we demonstrate that this framework accommodates interacting CFTs across the entire spectrum of couplings. Specifically, we show that the information-theoretic bounds on entanglement entropy are saturated in the limit of large couplings, whereas they remain unsaturated for weak couplings.

This paper presents a concise critique of the article "A Universal Framework for Pricing Asian Options Under Markov Processes" by Linetski and Lin, highlighting several inaccuracies and proposing appropriate remedies.

We present a new investigation into the diffuse gamma-ray emission originating from galaxy clusters, utilizing data from the Fermi-LAT mission. Our analysis employs a comprehensive model that accounts for the combined effects of intracluster medium (ICM) cosmic rays (CRs) and extragalactic background light (EBL) interactions. By leveraging the latest observations of the ICR's density and temperature profiles, alongside updated estimates for the CR-to-ICM density ratio and the EBL intensity, we calculate the expected gamma-ray flux. Our findings indicate that the predicted flux aligns with the lower limits observed by Fermi-LAT, suggesting that the actual ICR density may exceed current estimates by a factor of 2 to 3. Additionally, we demonstrate that the gamma-ray signal from galaxy clusters is highly sensitive to the EBL intensity, offering a potential method to constrain the EBL through future Fermi-LAT measurements.

We investigate how primordial fluctuations evolve when their wavelengths are sub-horizon at the onset of inflation, a scenario that generates an oscillatory signal in the primordial power spectrum. This signal is characterized by a frequency that increases exponentially with conformal time and a damping envelope that decays as a power law. We demonstrate that these oscillations can be analytically derived for a wide range of initial conditions and subsequently incorporated into both the Boltzmann code CLASS and the PICOLA library. Our implementation allows for the computation of the CMB temperature power spectrum, including the integrated contribution of primordial gravitational waves. We illustrate that these features enable the detection of the "cosmological collider" phenomenon even when modes re-enter the horizon after inflation has concluded. Furthermore, we examine the impact of this signal on primordial gravitational wave detection, noting that the cosmological collider leaves distinct imprints on the B-mode polarization spectrum.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have become a cornerstone of computer vision, yet their internal mechanisms remain opaque. To address this, researchers have developed various visualization techniques to interpret these "black-box" models. A common strategy involves generating class-specific input images to observe how the model reacts, but such approaches often fail to explain the model's behavior on actual data. This paper introduces a new method that leverages filter sensitivity to specific visual features to generate explanations for CNN predictions. By analyzing how filter responses change in relation to variations in an input image, we can pinpoint the specific visual elements that drive the model's decisions. This approach offers a more granular and detailed interpretation compared to earlier methods.

Phonon-mediated interactions are widely recognized as a mechanism for superconductivity in two-dimensional cuprates, yet their role in three-dimensional perovskite cuprates remains debated. This study presents a theoretical analysis of phonon-induced interactions in one-dimensional cuprates, revealing a long-range attractive potential between charge carriers. This potential is notably stronger than the conventional BCS interaction and arises from the coupling of charge carriers with longitudinal optical (LO) phonons. We demonstrate that these LO phonons generate an attractive force between holes, which is significantly more potent than the Debye phonon effect. Furthermore, we show that the strength of this interaction is highly sensitive to the distance separating the holes. Finally, we discuss the potential implications of these findings for one-dimensional cuprates.

This paper introduces a novel structural discovery algorithm for causal graphs, designed to handle datasets containing high levels of noise and redundant features. The proposed method is grounded in the theory of causal graphs and incorporates a new scoring mechanism for conditional independence tests. We evaluated this algorithm using simulated data and real-world data from the MPHIA individual dataset. Results indicate that the method outperforms existing state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of accuracy.

The skyrmion lattice in Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ is unstable at room temperature, yet it exhibits a robust topological phase characterized by a pronounced topological Hall effect. This study reveals that elevated temperatures induce a gradual degradation of the topological phase, which aligns with the progressive dissolution of the skyrmion lattice. This topological melting occurs over a temperature range of 200–300 K, a behavior that mirrors the phase transitions observed in other magnetic systems.

This paper introduces a selective overview of high-dimensional dynamic variable models, emphasizing linear structures where both covariates and response variables evolve over time. It examines the challenges of estimating the relationship matrix in this context, specifically addressing the hurdles posed by dimensionality and temporal autocorrelation. Furthermore, the text highlights the critical importance of model selection and variable identification. Finally, the authors outline a specific subset of their research on high-dimensional dynamic linear models, exploring various strategies for estimating the unknown relationship matrix under diverse assumptions, while also investigating the challenges of variable and model selection within this framework.

This work introduces a novel method for addressing the intersection of finding a common fixed point for a countable family of nonexpansive mappings and solving an equilibrium problem within a Hilbert space. We demonstrate that our findings generalize and extend several existing results in the literature related to these problems.

To address this, we utilize mean-field models to analyze the dynamo properties of three-dimensional convection simulations. We report on ALMA observations of the galaxy NGC4945, revealing a compact, elongated molecular feature extending approximately 100 pc along the galactic disk. This structure is elongated by a factor of 3 and exhibits a velocity gradient of 10 km/s across its length. The region displays a high column density of $N(\text{H}_2) \approx 10^{23} \text{ cm}^{-2}$ and a dense core with a mass of $M \approx 10^5 M_\odot$ at a density of $n(\text{H}_2) \approx 10^6 \text{ cm}^{-3}$. The observed kinematics are consistent with a tidal tail formed by a recent interaction between NGC4945 and a smaller companion galaxy. The presence of such a massive molecular clump in the tail suggests that tidal forces can trigger significant star formation within the stripped gas.

Quasilinear diffusion serves as a vital tool for modeling the neoclassical transport of particles and momentum in magnetized plasmas, as well as the collisional energy exchange between species. This study introduces a Galerkin solver designed to address quasilinear frameworks, featuring the preservation of key physical invariants, including the total number of particles, energy, and the non-negative entropy production rate. The proposed methodology employs a Galerkin approach for the distribution function while utilizing finite volumes to resolve the kinetic equation driving the evolution of quasilinear coefficients. The authors present a comprehensive analysis of the proposed algorithm, demonstrating its robustness through various numerical tests.

We introduce a novel family of variable-stepsize second-order implicit midpoint (SDIMSIM) schemes designed for standard differential equations. These methods integrate smoothly with existing variable-stepsize first-order explicit schemes, such as the classic explicit Euler method. We provide a local error analysis for the new family and, for the initial analysis of a specific subcase, extend the discussion to include stability investigations.
This work establishes findings on the exponential stability of $C_0$-semigroups within the context of Banach spaces.

This study introduces MuMuPy, an open-source Python library designed to compute the optical cross sections for elastic $\lceil\mu^+\mu^-\rceil$-nucleus and elastic $\lceil\mu^+\mu^-\rceil$-atom interactions, as well as the reduced bound-state wave functions for $\lceil\mu^+\mu^-\rceil$-atom systems. The code employs the non-relativistic Born approximation to model $\lceil\mu^+\mu^-\rceil$-atom scattering events, utilizing a relativistic point-like approximation for the bound state. The accuracy of the calculated results is validated against existing experimental data and theoretical models.

This paper investigates the optimal portfolio problem for a power utility function that depends on both absolute and relative wealth. The objective is to maximize the expected utility of terminal wealth at a fixed horizon, where the wealth dynamics are governed by a stochastic differential equation driven by Brownian motion and subject to box constraints on portfolio holdings. The analysis covers two scenarios: first, an open-loop control setting where investment strategies are non-adapted to information flow, and second, an open-loop setting where strategies are adapted. The paper derives necessary conditions for optimality using the stochastic maximum principle and proposes numerical methods to solve the resulting system of backward-forward stochastic differential equations. The study demonstrates that the optimal open-loop strategy is unique and exhibits a singular perturbation structure, converging toward the open-loop solution as the wealth gap between investor and benchmark diminishes. Furthermore, it is shown that the open-loop strategy is asymptotically optimal when the investor's wealth approaches that of the benchmark.

This review examines the intergalactic medium (IGM) within dwarf galaxies, a component that is often overlooked in broader discussions of the IGM. Dwarf galaxies are significant because they are the primary producers of IGM and host the IGM in large quantities. We examine the IGM in dwarf galaxies across three categories: those that are currently forming stars, those that have ceased star formation, and those that have never hosted star formation. We also explore the IGM in dwarf galaxies that have undergone starbursts and those that have experienced multiple episodes of star formation. We discuss the IGM's physical characteristics, its chemical makeup, and its connection to the galaxy's star formation history. We also address the IGM's role in regulating star formation and the feedback mechanisms involved. We conclude by outlining future research directions.

We investigate the impact of coupling local bosons to fermionic quasiparticles within a one-dimensional fermi-liquid framework. Our analysis reveals that, contrary to expectations, such interactions can destabilize fermionic quasiparticles, leading to a quasiparticle-free ground state. This phenomenon is illustrated by a model featuring a charge degree of freedom subject to a transverse magnetic field alongside spinless fermions, where charge fluctuations act as local bosons. In this setup, quasiparticles undergo a first-order transition into a state devoid of them, a behavior confirmed by both mean-field theory and exact diagonalization. Furthermore, we examine the implications of this transition on the system's thermodynamic properties and its dynamical response.

This work introduces a class of groups known as the braided-Thompson groups, which are generated by braided generators and act on braided binary trees. We demonstrate that these groups are simple, finitely presented, divergence 1, and possess a solvable word problem. Additionally, we prove they are not finitely dimensional, do not fall into the class of groups with finitely many conjugacy classes of finitely generated subgroups, and fail to be the universal central extension of the generalised Thompson groups.

This study explores the effectiveness of fine-tuning the entire Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture, specifically the combination of a document retriever and a generator, for question-answering tasks. We evaluate two document retrieval models, including a pre-trained Dual Encoder (DPR) retriever, alongside two large language models capable of generating answers. Our findings reveal that the dual-stage retrieval system significantly outperforms standard methods that rely solely on a generator's internal memory for answering questions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that fine-tuning the dual-stage architecture yields superior performance compared to fine-tuning only the generator within that framework.

This study examines the asymptotic behavior of monic orthogonal polynomials within a logarithmic influence framework on $[-1,1]$, where weight functions are defined as $w_{\alpha,\beta}(x) = (1-x)^{\alpha}(1+x)^{\beta}\log^k\left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right)$ for $\alpha, \beta > -1$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}_0$. The analysis derives the precise asymptotic form of the leading coefficient for these polynomials. Furthermore, it establishes the necessary conditions for orthogonality involving influence terms of the type $\log^k\left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right)$ for all $k \in \mathbb{N}_0$.

Gaining a deeper understanding of the labor market on Mechanical Turk (MTurk) is essential for optimizing the assignment of Human Intelligence Tasks (HITs). This study examines the challenges associated with identifying skilled workers within this vast ecosystem. We present findings from an experiment involving 1,000 HITs, which were completed by 1,000 individuals across 10 distinct task categories. The results indicate that locating even a single high-quality submission can be exceptionally difficult, particularly for tasks requiring specialized knowledge. Additionally, we observe that many participants engage in "free-riding" by copying others' work, a behavior that is more prevalent when the likelihood of detection is low. Finally, we explore the impact of reusing worker identities, noting that such actions can lead to significant quality degradation.

Video retrieval involves aligning textual queries with relevant video clips, a task where Transformer models have proven effective. Nevertheless, these models often struggle with the prohibitive computational costs associated with self-attention mechanisms and are prone to focusing on irrelevant information. To address these limitations, we introduce TS2-Net, a novel architecture designed to enhance both the efficiency and accuracy of retrieval. First, we replace standard self-attention with a new Token Shift and Selection (TSS) module that significantly boosts computational efficiency. Second, we implement a dual-level loss function to refine feature representations, thereby suppressing noise and boosting overall accuracy. Third, we develop an adaptive query encoding mechanism that dynamically adjusts the encoding of textual inputs. Empirical evaluations on two prominent datasets demonstrate that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques in both performance and efficiency.

We investigate the phenomenology of a new neutral scalar boson $S$ that couples to the top quark, which can induce both flavor-changing neutral currents (FCNC) involving bottom quarks and standard flavor-conserving neutral currents (NC) involving top quarks. Specifically, we examine how this scenario impacts the rare decays $t \to cZ$ and $t \to c\gamma$, as well as the Higgs production via top-quark loops. Our analysis demonstrates that the FCNC decay $t \to cZ$ imposes stringent limits on the model's parameter space, which are comparable to those derived from the Higgs production rate. Furthermore, we assess the feasibility of observing the $t \to cZ$ signal at the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC).

This study examines a directed hybrid random graph model that integrates both preferential attachment and uniform attachment mechanisms. We demonstrate that this hybrid graph possesses a minimum degree of 1 and a maximum degree of $O(\log n)$ with high probability. Furthermore, we establish that the degree distribution follows a power law with an exponent of $\gamma = 3/2$ under conditions of high probability. Additionally, we prove that the hybrid graph contains a minimum of $\Omega(n)$ cycles and a maximum of $O(n)$ cycles with high probability.

This paper introduces a wireless disturbance identification (WDI) framework utilizing a multi-label convolutional neural network (MLCNN). The proposed approach is designed to detect disturbances within audio streams and concurrently classify their specific types. To achieve this, the study presents a novel multi-label loss function optimized for imbalanced datasets, which is integrated into the MLCNN architecture. The framework's effectiveness is validated through extensive experiments on a newly created dataset comprising 1,000 distinct audio samples, each 10 seconds in duration. Results demonstrate that the MLCNN surpasses existing methods in both disturbance detection accuracy and multi-label classification performance.

This study investigates the behavior of scalar particles within a Som-Raychaudhuri spacetime characterized by a cosmic string that possesses linear momentum and dislocation. The analysis focuses on the interplay between the spacetime's vorticity and the particle's mass, alongside the relationship between electric charge and energy. The relativistic scalar field equation is solved using the de Broglie-Bohm framework, yielding a complex Klein-Gordon wave function. From this, key dynamical quantities—including the electric charge density, energy density, probability current, quantum potential, and the particle's trajectory—are derived. The results demonstrate that cosmic string dislocation influences both the charge-energy correlation and the mass-vorticity correlation. Furthermore, the particle's path is observed to be a helix, a direct consequence of the spacetime's vorticity.

This work presents a counterexample to an inquiry raised by D. S. Dubois in 1982, demonstrating that measure algebras with unit ball norm topology are not necessarily uniformly bounded. As a direct consequence, we establish that measure algebras equipped on their unit balls with the metric topology are not necessarily complete. This finding further clarates that the property of being complete is not preserved under taking subalgebras. In addition, we derive a necessary and sufficient condition for a measure algebra to possess the locally usual measure topology, thereby providing a comprehensive characterization of locally standard measure spaces.

The polarization of the recoil proton in deeply virtual Compton scattering (DVCS) offers a novel means to distinguish between the DVCS and Bethe-Heitler (BH) amplitudes. This paper examines the kinematical range where this polarization remains robust against BH dominance, thereby enabling a precise extraction of the generalized polarized parton distribution function, $g_T(x, \zeta)$. Our analysis indicates that, within the Jefferson Lab 12 GeV energy regime, this observable is most sensitive to $g_T$ when the longitudinal momentum transfer squared, $-t$, falls between 0.5 and 1.5 GeV$^2$.

This paper introduces a new framework for classifying synthetic intelligence (SI) applications, built upon a refined definition of the term. We propose that SI refers to a system's capacity to generate a specific type of intelligence by utilizing a distinct set of capabilities. This framework offers a refined categorization of SI uses, which we demonstrate through a comprehensive survey of existing literature. By analyzing these sources, we identify a total of 128 unique SI applications and organize them according to our proposed model. Finally, we outline future research trajectories and suggest potential avenues for further investigation.

We investigate the thermal behavior of a Bose-Hubbard model featuring nearest-neighbor hopping and spin-orbit coupling, which is solved using high-temperature and finite-temperature perturbation theory. Spin-orbit coupling induces a structural modulation in the superfluid's phase diagram, creating distinct regions of gapped and gapless superfluidity. Our analysis reveals that within the gapless regime, a superfluid-to-normal transition occurs at a temperature scaling linearly with the interaction strength. Conversely, in the gapped regime, this transition temperature scales quadratically with interactions. Additionally, we examine the effects of disorder on the superfluid's stability.

We investigate the connections between a finite abelian group $G$ and its associated Cayley graph $\Gamma$ when the generating sets differ. Specifically, we demonstrate that if $G$ is cyclic, the number of edges in $\Gamma$ is sufficient to determine $G$' isomorphism class. Furthermore, we establish that the graphs associated with non-isomorphic finite abelian groups are distinct even when they share the same number of edges. Finally, we examine the behavior of these graphs under graph-theoretic degenerations.

We investigate holographic duals of solutions to massive Type IIA supergravity in eleven dimensions, focusing on low-dimensional AdS spaces. By analyzing these massive Type IIA supergravity configurations, we derive novel holographic dual descriptions involving AdS spaces in low dimensions. Specifically, we examine AdS₃/CFT₂ and AdS₄/CFT₃ dualities, where AdS₃/CFT₂ involves three-dimensional anti-de Sitter spaces paired with two-dimensional conformal field theories, while AdS₄/CFT₃ involves four-dimensional anti-de Sitter spaces paired with three-dimensional conformal field theories. Through this analysis, we uncover new holographic duals arising from Type IIA supergravity in massive eleven dimensions, focusing on AdS spaces in low dimensions. For AdS₃/CFT₂ dualities, we identify novel three-dimensional supergravity backgrounds dual to two-dimensional conformal field theories, while for AdS₄/CFT₃ dualities, we identify novel four-dimensional supergravity backgrounds dual to three-dimensional conformal field theories. These discoveries expand our understanding of holographic dualities in supergravity, particularly in low-dimensional settings, by revealing new connections between massive Type IIA supergravity configurations in eleven dimensions and lower-dimensional anti-de Sitter/conformal field theory pairs.

We introduce a novel kernel construction technique for Gaussian processes that derives the hyperparameters of a sum-of-products form directly from elementary mathematical expressions. The anticipated luminosity of 10³⁴ cm⁻²s⁻¹ at a proposed muon collider is expected to generate intense beam-induced noise, potentially compromising detector performance. This paper outlines a strategy to mitigate such effects by employing a tailored bunch-by-bunch instrumentation approach. By measuring the noise source directly at the point of interaction, we can isolate and subtract it from the detector readout. This method relies on a high-speed data acquisition system capable of recording both the signal and background with precise timing synchronization. The study evaluates the feasibility of this approach for various experimental setups, including those utilizing silicon trackers, scintillating trackers, and electromagnetic calorimeters.

Sparsity has long been a cornerstone technique for enhancing model interpretability and efficiency, yet existing approaches are constrained by the need for discrete weight pruning or reliance on heuristic search methods. This work introduces a novel framework for achieving continuous sparsity by formulating the problem as a regularized optimal transportation task. By applying regularized entropic regularization to the transportation formulation, we derive a novel, differentiable sparsity-inducing regularizer. This approach offers a flexible alternative to traditional entropy regularization, which struggles to effectively promote actual sparsity. We demonstrate that the proposed method can be seamlessly integrated into standard deep learning architectures and training workflows. Empirical evaluations on various classification and regression tasks confirm that the method successfully generates sparse weights while maintaining model accuracy.

This study investigates the evolution of a two-dimensional (2D) weakly interacting bosonic gas as it transitions from the non-interacting regime to one of strong repulsion. We demonstrate that, contrary to expectations, the excitations of such a system can undergo a crossover from bosonic to fermionic behavior. Specifically, we identify a critical interaction strength where the collective excitations acquire fermionic characteristics, marked by a non-zero effective mass and a Pauli exclusion principle. These findings are substantiated by numerical simulations using the time-dependent variational principle with a Slater-Jastrow ansatz, which aligns closely with results from quantum Monte Carlo methods.

Test smells are code issues that impair the efficacy of testing, yet their impact on testing effectiveness varies by context. This study examines the severity of various test smells from a developer's viewpoint, specifically focusing on how they influence the effort required to locate and fix test failures. Data was gathered through a questionnaire administered to 100 participants, including both professional developers and students. The findings indicate that developers perceive certain test smells as significantly more severe than others. Furthermore, the research establishes a correlation between these perceived severities and the actual reduction in debugging time, supporting the hypothesis that developers' intuitions align with the objective benefits of addressing these issues.

This work examines a nonconvex integro-differential equation arising from the study of a nonconvex brushing process. We establish the existence and uniqueness of a weak solution, which is both differentiable with respect to time and the spatial variable. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this solution possesses specific smoothness characteristics in both temporal and spatial dimensions. The study also includes a thorough analysis of the associated stationary problem. Finally, we explore potential applications within the context of image segmentation.

This paper introduces the KKMCee event generator, designed to simulate lepton and quark pair production via electron-positron annihilation, complete with the emission of multiple photons. The primary focus targets the on-resonance production of charged lepton pairs, specifically the $t\bar{t}$ system, which is a primary objective for future high-energy $e^+e^-$ colliders. The generated events are intended for use in experimental analyses and theoretical studies, with a specific emphasis on the differential cross-sections for quark pair creation. The simulation accounts for the full QED radiative corrections, including initial-state radiation, final-state radiation, and interference terms, as well as the decay of the intermediate vector boson. The accuracy of the program has been validated against results from the established BHWIDE Monte Carlo package.

Accurately quantifying heart rate variability (HRV) is vital for assessing cardiovascular health and predicting disease risk. This study introduces a novel deep learning architecture, Tiramisu, designed to extract inter-beat intervals (IBIs) from single-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) signals. The model's design features a multi-scale encoder-decoder framework that integrates residual blocks and skip connections to capture diverse feature representations while mitigating gradient vanishing. Trained on the PTB-BX dataset, the approach achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 15.85 ms and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 19.85 ms. These results demonstrate a significant improvement over prior methods, underscoring the model's potential for high-precision IBI estimation.

Graphs serve as a potent mechanism for modeling intricate real-world phenomena, such as social interactions, biological systems, and information networks. While node embeddings have proven highly effective for graph representation learning, most existing methods are restricted to static graphs and fail to capture temporal dynamics. In contrast, embedding evolving graphs holds significant promise for modeling time-varying data. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of current approaches to embedding evolving graphs, categorizing existing techniques into three primary frameworks: temporal graph learning, temporal factorization, and temporal link prediction. We critically examine the strengths and limitations of each approach, identify key unresolved challenges, and propose promising avenues for future research.

The $^7$H nucleus is a highly unstable system with a half-life of approximately $10^{-22}$ s, rendering it impossible to characterize as a conventional bound state. Instead, it is best understood as a $^3$H+4n unbound configuration. By employing a three-body model that accounts for the sequential decay of this unbound system, we have calculated the $E1$ photoabsorption cross section for $^7$H. Our findings indicate that the photoabsorption peak is dominated by the excitation of four neutrons, with the $^3$H core remaining essentially stationary.

We introduce a deep generative model designed to learn an optimal latent representation that minimizes the Sinkhorn divergence between real data and model-generated samples. This framework is designed to be versatile, accommodating various probabilistic models and a wide range of data types, including images, audio, and text. We demonstrate the model's efficacy through experiments on three major domains: generating realistic images and text, as well as creating synthetic audio.

In the United Kingdom, local authorities are responsible for executing the core contact tracing functions, even though the National COVID Tracing Centre provides the underlying technology. This study evaluates how the varying capacities of these local entities influence the overall effectiveness of the system. We introduce a multi-agent model that simulates interactions between the National Tracing Centre and local authorities, incorporating a novel representation of a dynamic, non-uniform network of infected individuals and their contacts. This network evolves as agents recover, are traced, or are removed from the system. Our analysis reveals that disparities in local execution capabilities can result in substantial variations in transmission rates. Furthermore, we examine the effects of different tracing strategies and the optimal timing for deploying the system.

We determine its distance to be 1.02 ± 0.04 kpc, its age to be 1.00 ± 0.20 Gyr, and its metallicity to be [Fe/H] = -0.03 ± 0.05. These findings are consistent with previous research. We also identify a binary fraction of 10.00 ± 0.05% among the cluster members.
